PART 1

What a crystal is

Solids differ from liquids and gases in one respect above all: how their particles are arranged. This part builds the vocabulary of the whole chapter: order, lattice, basis, unit cell, the 14 Bravais lattices and symmetry.

Crystalline, amorphous and polycrystalline solids

In a crystalline solid the constituent particles (atoms, ions or molecules) sit in a regular pattern that repeats over long distances: long-range order. An amorphous solid has order only over a few particle diameters (short-range order), like a liquid that has been frozen in place. A polycrystalline solid is a mass of tiny crystals (grains) fused at random orientations. Watch the three outcomes below.

❄ Cool it🔥 Melt it
Slow cooling → crystalQuench → amorphousMany nuclei → polycrystal
Crystalline. Cooled slowly, the particles have time to find the lowest-energy arrangement: a regular pattern that repeats through the whole sample (long-range order).

Amorphous solids are sometimes called pseudo-solids or super-cooled liquids because they lack a sharp melting point and a true long-range pattern. Quartz is crystalline SiO₂; quartz glass, with the same composition, is amorphous.

Anisotropy
Measure a physical property (electrical or thermal conductivity, refractive index, mechanical strength) along different directions. In a crystal the value changes with direction because the particles are arranged differently along different lines: the blue curve. In an amorphous solid the arrangement looks statistically the same from every direction, so the value does not change: the violet circle. A polycrystal is isotropic on a large scale because its grains point every way.

Classifying crystalline solids by their binding

What the particles are, and what holds them, decides hardness, melting point and electrical behaviour. Try the two interactive demonstrations: electrons carry current in a metal, while a struck ionic crystal shatters.

JEE traps
  • A crystal is anisotropic; an amorphous solid and a polycrystalline sample are isotropic on a large scale.
  • Glass has no sharp melting point and no definite heat of fusion. Quartz glass and quartz are different solids with the same formula.
  • Ionic solids conduct only when molten or dissolved. Metals conduct as solids. Graphite conducts because of its delocalised layers, not because it is metallic.
  • Hydrogen-bonded molecular solids (ice) are molecular, not ionic or covalent.

Lattice, basis and unit cell

To describe a crystal, separate where the repeating units are from what they are. A lattice is an array of points in which every point has exactly the same surroundings. The basis is the atom, or group of atoms, attached to each lattice point. Crystal structure = lattice + basis. A unit cell is the parallelogram (in 3D, parallelepiped) spanned by the lattice vectors a, b (and c); translating it fills all space.

Attach a basis to every point
ObliqueRectangularCentred rectangularSquareHexagonal
Hexagonal lattice. a = b, γ = 120°. The shaded parallelogram is a unit cell with sides a and b and angle γ: copies of it, translated, fill the whole plane.
Edge a
8.0 units
Edge b
8.0 units
Angle γ
120°
Points per cell
1 (primitive)

There are five distinct plane lattices. A cell with exactly one lattice point is primitive; a cell with more (the centred rectangle) is non-primitive but is chosen because it shows the rectangular symmetry.

Lattice point is not the same as atom
A lattice point is a mathematical point. A real crystal can have many atoms per lattice point (a basis of 2 in diamond, a whole molecule in a protein crystal), and two different structures can share one lattice.

Choosing a repeat unit: two-dimensional NaCl

The unit cell is the smallest repeating unit that shows the full symmetry of the crystal. Take a layer of NaCl and try different squares. A valid cell must be identical from one to the next and must fill the plane with no gaps; where you put the origin is largely a matter of taste.

(b) Cl at corners(c) Na at corners(d) origin off-ion(e) half-size, tilted(f) isolated squares(f) unlike squares
Valid repeat unit
A square of side 2 with Cl⁻ at every corner and at the centre. Every square in the tiling is identical, and adjacent squares share edges and corners. This is a valid repeat unit and shows the full symmetry.
The NaCl cell in three dimensions
In three dimensions the NaCl unit cell is based on (b) or (c) rather than (e), because only those show the cubic symmetry. One valid choice has Na⁺ at the corners and face centres with Cl⁻ at the edge centres and the body centre; an equally valid cell swaps the two ions. The cell is cubic: a = b = c and α = β = γ = 90°.

Seven crystal systems and fourteen Bravais lattices

In three dimensions a unit cell is described by three edges a, b, c and three angles α (between b and c), β (between a and c) and γ (between a and b). Only seven shapes of cell fill space with different symmetry, the crystal systems. Placing extra lattice points at the centre of the cell (I), at the centres of all faces (F), or at the centres of one pair of faces (C) gives further distinct lattices. Auguste Bravais showed that exactly 14 exist.

Counting and remembering the systems
All seven systems have a primitive lattice. Body-centred (I): 3 (cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic). Face-centred (F): 2 (cubic, orthorhombic). End-centred (C): 2 (orthorhombic, monoclinic). Orthorhombic is the only system with all four types, and triclinic is the least symmetrical. Order to remember: C – T – O – M – H – R – Tri (cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, monoclinic, hexagonal, rhombohedral, triclinic). There are 32 crystal classes in all, of which these 7 are the independent systems.
JEE traps
  • There are 14 Bravais lattices in 7 systems. Counts: cubic 3, tetragonal 2, orthorhombic 4, hexagonal 1, rhombohedral 1, monoclinic 2, triclinic 1.
  • Cubic has P, I, F only; a C-centred cubic lattice would simply be a primitive tetragonal one. Tetragonal has P and I only for the same reason (F reduces to I).
  • Only orthorhombic has all four types P, C, I, F.
  • Hexagonal: a = b ≠ c with γ = 120°. Rhombohedral: a = b = c with α = β = γ ≠ 90°.
  • Remember the angles: α is opposite to a (between b and c).

Density, packing efficiency and every X-ray calculation need the volume of the cell. For a cube it is a3a^3a3; for the other six systems the edges and angles enter. All seven results come from one general expression, derived below.

Symmetry of the cube

A symmetry element is a point, line or plane about which an operation leaves the crystal looking unchanged. 1.1 The solid state and structural order

A solid has a definite volume and resists shear because its constituent particles occupy positions around which only limited thermal motion is possible. The word constituent is deliberately broad: the repeating entities may be atoms, ions, molecules or extended covalent fragments. Solid-state chemistry therefore begins with the spatial order of these entities, not merely with the chemical formula.

In a crystalline solid, equivalent environments recur by translation through macroscopic distances. In an amorphous solid, the nearest-neighbour arrangement may be reproducible over a few interatomic distances, but no translation reproduces the entire structure over long range.

Macroscopic behaviour follows from microscopic order.
FeatureCrystalline solidAmorphous solid
OrderLong-range periodic orderShort-range order only
External formMay develop regular faces when growth is unhinderedNo necessary geometrical form
MeltingSharp melting temperature for a pure, well-ordered crystalSoftens through a temperature range
Heat of fusionDefinite at the melting pointNo single sharply defined value
CleavageOften along definite crystallographic planesIrregular fracture
X-ray diffractionSharp Bragg reflectionsBroad diffuse maxima
Directional propertiesMay be anisotropicMacroscopically isotropic in the ordinary case
Do not confuse rigidity with crystallinity

Glass is rigid on an ordinary time scale but lacks long-range translational periodicity. Calling glass a ‘supercooled liquid’ is a historical simplification; for examination purposes, classify it as an amorphous solid.

1.2 Anisotropy, isotropy and polycrystalline materials

A physical property is anisotropic when its measured value depends on crystallographic direction. Electrical conductivity, refractive index, thermal expansion and mechanical strength may differ along different axes because the arrangement and bonding of particles differ with direction.

P[uvw]≠P[u′v′w′]P_{[uvw]}\neq P_{[u'v'w']}P[uvw]​=P[u′v′w′]​

A directional property PPP can have different values along two crystal directions.

A single crystal can display anisotropy clearly. A polycrystalline specimen contains many small crystallites or grains. If those grains are randomly oriented, their directional responses average out and the bulk specimen may appear isotropic. If processing produces preferred orientation, or texture, the bulk material can remain anisotropic.

MaterialMicroscopic descriptionTypical macroscopic response
Single crystalOne continuous orientationAnisotropy can be measured directly
Random polycrystalMany randomly oriented grainsApproximately isotropic average
Textured polycrystalMany grains with preferred orientationDirectional bulk properties
Amorphous solidNo long-range periodic axesUsually isotropic
1
Worked example

Recognising polycrystalline averaging

A metal foil consists of many cubic crystallites with random orientations. One crystallite is elastically anisotropic. Must the foil show the same anisotropy?

  1. The response of each grain depends on its orientation.
  2. Random orientations sample all directions statistically.
  3. The measured bulk response is therefore an orientational average, unless the foil has texture.
No. A random polycrystal may be macroscopically isotropic even though every grain is anisotropic.

1.3 Classification of crystalline solids by bonding

The traditional classification identifies the particles at lattice sites and the dominant force that holds the crystal together. Real solids can have mixed bonding, so the categories are models rather than impermeable compartments.

ClassConstituent particlesDominant interactionCharacteristic propertiesExamples
IonicCations and anionsElectrostatic attractionHard, brittle, high melting; insulating as solids but conducting when molten or dissolvedNaCl, MgO, CaF2_22​
Molecular—non-polarMolecules or atomsLondon dispersionSoft, low melting, volatileAr, I2_22​, solid CO2_22​
Molecular—polarPolar moleculesDipole–dipole forcesModerate melting; electrical insulatorsSO2_22​, HCl
Hydrogen-bonded molecularMoleculesHydrogen bondingHigher melting than comparable molecular solidsIce, urea
Covalent networkAtoms connected throughout the latticeDirectional covalent bondsVery hard, very high melting; usually non-conductingDiamond, SiC, SiO2_22​
MetallicMetal kernels and delocalised electronsMetallic bondingMalleable, ductile, lustrous, conductingCu, Fe, Na
Graphite is an important exception

Graphite is a covalent solid that conducts strongly within its layers because π\piπ electrons are delocalised. Its conductivity and mechanical properties are highly anisotropic.

2
Worked example

Bonding model from properties

A solid is soft, melts near room temperature and does not conduct in either the solid or liquid state. Which broad class is most likely?

  1. Low melting and softness exclude a three-dimensional ionic or covalent network.
  2. Failure to conduct in the melt argues against a simple ionic solid.
  3. Weak intermolecular attractions are consistent with a molecular crystal.
A molecular solid is the most likely classification.

1.4 Lattice, basis and crystal structure

A space lattice is an infinite periodic array of equivalent geometrical points. Every lattice point has the same surroundings as every other lattice point. A lattice point is not automatically an atom: it may represent an ion, a molecule, or the reference point of a multi-particle motif.

crystal structure=lattice+basis\text{crystal structure}=\text{lattice}+\text{basis}crystal structure=lattice+basis

Attach the same basis, in the same orientation, to every lattice point.

The basis or motif is the atom or group of atoms associated with each lattice point. Two crystals can possess the same Bravais lattice but different bases and therefore different structures. Conversely, a drawing that contains a point at the body centre is not necessarily a body-centred Bravais lattice; the corner and centre sites must be translationally equivalent.

The CsCl test

In CsCl, a Cs+^++ ion and a Cl−^-− ion occupy corner and body-centre positions. Because the two positions are chemically different, translation by (12,12,12)(\tfrac12,\tfrac12,\tfrac12)(21​,21​,21​) does not reproduce an equivalent point. CsCl is therefore not a BCC Bravais lattice.

1.5 Unit cell and lattice parameters

A unit cell is a finite region whose translations generate the entire lattice without gaps or overlaps. A primitive cell contains exactly one lattice point in total. A conventional cell may contain more than one lattice point because it is chosen to display symmetry more clearly.

A three-dimensional unit cell is described by edge lengths aaa, bbb, ccc and interaxial angles α\alphaα, β\betaβ, γ\gammaγ. By convention, α\alphaα is the angle between bbb and ccc, β\betaβ between aaa and ccc, and γ\gammaγ between aaa and bbb.

Vcell=abc1+2cos⁡αcos⁡βcos⁡γ−cos⁡2α−cos⁡2β−cos⁡2γV_{cell}=abc\sqrt{1+2\cos\alpha\cos\beta\cos\gamma-\cos^2\alpha-\cos^2\beta-\cos^2\gamma}Vcell​=abc1+2cosαcosβcosγ−cos2α−cos2β−cos2γ​

For an orthogonal cell, α=β=γ=90∘\alpha=\beta=\gamma=90^\circα=β=γ=90∘ and the volume reduces to abcabcabc. For a cubic cell, a=b=ca=b=ca=b=c, so V=a3V=a^3V=a3.

TermMeaning
Lattice pointA geometrical point with an environment equivalent to every other lattice point
Basis or motifChemical content attached to each lattice point
Primitive cellA cell containing one lattice point in total
Conventional cellA symmetry-revealing cell that may contain several lattice points
Unit-cell parametersa,b,c,α,β,γa,b,c,\alpha,\beta,\gammaa,b,c,α,β,γ
3
Worked example

Primitive cell versus one atom

A primitive cell of a molecular crystal contains one lattice point. The basis at each point is a molecule containing 12 atoms. How many atoms are associated with the primitive cell?

  1. A primitive cell contains one lattice point, not necessarily one atom.
  2. Each point carries one 12-atom molecular basis.
The primitive cell contains one molecule, hence 12 atoms.

2.1 Fractional contribution of boundary particles

A particle exactly on a unit-cell boundary is shared by neighbouring cells. Its contribution to one selected cell equals the fraction of its surrounding space that lies inside that cell.

PositionNumber of equivalent cells sharing the positionContribution to one cell
Corner81/81/81/8
Edge centre41/41/41/4
Face centre21/21/21/2
Body centre1111
Completely internal site1111
Ncell=Nc8+Ne4+Nf2+Nb+NiN_{cell}=\frac{N_c}{8}+\frac{N_e}{4}+\frac{N_f}{2}+N_b+N_iNcell​=8Nc​​+4Ne​​+2Nf​​+Nb​+Ni​

The formula counts any specified species. Apply it separately to each chemically distinct atom or ion when determining the formula of a unit cell.

1
Worked example

Counting a mixed cell

Species A occupies all corners and all face centres; species B occupies all edge centres and one body centre. Determine the formula.

  1. A: 8(1/8)+6(1/2)=1+3=48(1/8)+6(1/2)=1+3=48(1/8)+6(1/2)=1+3=4.
  2. B: 12(1/4)+1=3+1=412(1/4)+1=3+1=412(1/4)+1=3+1=4.
  3. The ratio A:B is 4:4=1:14:4=1:14:4=1:1.
The empirical formula is AB.

2.2 Primitive and centred conventional cells

Centring describes additional lattice points in a conventional cell. The added points must be equivalent to the corner points under lattice translation.

SymbolNameAdditional lattice pointsLattice points per conventional cell
PPrimitiveCorners only1
IBody-centredOne body centre2
FFace-centredCentres of all six faces4
C (or A/B)Base-centredCentres of one pair of opposite faces2
  • Representative I-centring translation: (12,12,12)(\tfrac12,\tfrac12,\tfrac12)(21​,21​,21​).
  • Independent F-centring translations: (12,12,0)(\tfrac12,\tfrac12,0)(21​,21​,0), (12,0,12)(\tfrac12,0,\tfrac12)(21​,0,21​) and (0,12,12)(0,\tfrac12,\tfrac12)(0,21​,21​).
  • A base-centred cell has only one opposite pair of centred faces; it is not face-centred.
Centring is not a contact rule

SC, BCC and FCC names specify translational equivalence. Sphere contact along an edge, body diagonal or face diagonal is a separate hard-sphere model used later.

2
Worked example

Lattice-point count

How many lattice points are contained in an F-centred conventional cell?

  1. Corners contribute 8×1/8=18\times 1/8=18×1/8=1.
  2. Face centres contribute 6×1/2=36\times 1/2=36×1/2=3.
An F-centred conventional cell contains 4 lattice points.

2.3 From one-dimensional lattices to three dimensions

In one dimension there is only one Bravais lattice: equally spaced points on a line. In two dimensions there are five Bravais lattices. Extending periodicity into three dimensions produces seven metric crystal systems and fourteen distinct Bravais lattices.

Squarea=ba=ba=b, γ=90∘\gamma=90^\circγ=90∘Primitive
Hexagonala=ba=ba=b, γ=120∘\gamma=120^\circγ=120∘Primitive

The common statement ‘five two-dimensional lattices’ counts primitive rectangular and centred rectangular separately. A centred square net can be redrawn as a smaller primitive square net rotated by 45∘45^\circ45∘, so it is not a new lattice.

Hexagonal angle convention

The two equal basal vectors are separated by 120∘120^\circ120∘ in the conventional hexagonal cell. A 60∘60^\circ60∘ choice can describe the same net with oppositely directed basis vectors, but exam tables use 120∘120^\circ120∘.

2.5 Fourteen Bravais lattices

Not every centring type creates a distinct lattice in every crystal system. Some centred descriptions can be transformed into a smaller primitive cell of another allowed type. After eliminating equivalent descriptions, exactly fourteen three-dimensional Bravais lattices remain.

Crystal systemAllowed Bravais latticesCount
CubicP, I, F3
TetragonalP, I2
OrthorhombicP, C, I, F4
HexagonalP1
TrigonalR1
MonoclinicP, C2
TriclinicP1
3+2+4+1+1+2+1=143+2+4+1+1+2+1=143+2+4+1+1+2+1=14
  • Orthorhombic is the only system that has P, C, I and F forms.
  • There are three body-centred Bravais lattices: cubic I, tetragonal I and orthorhombic I.
  • A structure type such as CsCl, NaCl or perovskite is not a Bravais-lattice name.
3
Worked example

Bravais-lattice integer

How many of the fourteen Bravais lattices are non-primitive?

  1. Cubic contributes I and F: 2.
  2. Tetragonal contributes I: 1.
  3. Orthorhombic contributes C, I and F: 3.
  4. Monoclinic contributes C: 1.
There are 2+1+3+1=72+1+3+1=72+1+3+1=7 non-primitive Bravais lattices.

2.6 Symmetry elements of a cube

The cube belongs to the highest-symmetry common crystal system. A geometrical symmetry element is a line, plane or point about which a symmetry operation can be performed.

ElementNumberDescription
C4C_4C4​ axes3Through centres of opposite faces
C3C_3C3​ axes4Along body diagonals
C2C_2C2​ axes6Through midpoints of opposite edges
Mirror planes93 axial planes and 6 diagonal planes
Centre of inversion1At the cube centre
3+4+6+9+1=233+4+6+9+1=233+4+6+9+1=23

This classroom count refers to geometrical elements, not the total number of symmetry operations.

Axes versus operations

A single C4C_4C4​ axis permits several rotations (90∘90^\circ90∘, 180∘180^\circ180∘, 270∘270^\circ270∘). Do not equate the number of axes with the number of rotational operations.

2.7 Fractional coordinates, directions and planes

Atomic positions are usually written as fractional coordinates (x,y,z)(x,y,z)(x,y,z), meaning r=xa+yb+zc\mathbf r=x\mathbf a+y\mathbf b+z\mathbf cr=xa+yb+zc. Coordinates differing by integers describe translationally equivalent positions. For example, (1,0,0)(1,0,0)(1,0,0) is equivalent to (0,0,0)(0,0,0)(0,0,0) in a periodic lattice.

NotationMeaningExample
[uvw][uvw][uvw]One crystallographic direction[110][110][110] is a face diagonal in a cubic cell
⟨uvw⟩\langle uvw\rangle⟨uvw⟩Family of symmetry-equivalent directions⟨100⟩\langle100\rangle⟨100⟩ contains the cubic edge directions
(hkl)(hkl)(hkl)One plane orientation(111)(111)(111) is one body-diagonal-normal plane
{hkl}\{hkl\}{hkl}Family of symmetry-equivalent planes{100}\{100\}{100} contains the six cube-face orientations

To obtain a direction index, subtract the fractional coordinates of the initial point from those of the final point, then clear fractions to the smallest integers. Direction indices describe a vector; they are not obtained by taking reciprocals.

4
Worked example

Direction from two points

Find the direction from (1/4,0,1/2)(1/4,0,1/2)(1/4,0,1/2) to (3/4,1/2,1/2)(3/4,1/2,1/2)(3/4,1/2,1/2).

  1. Displacement is (3/4−1/4,1/2−0,1/2−1/2)=(1/2,1/2,0)(3/4-1/4,1/2-0,1/2-1/2)=(1/2,1/2,0)(3/4−1/4,1/2−0,1/2−1/2)=(1/2,1/2,0).
  2. Clear fractions by multiplying by 2.
The direction is [110][110][110].

2.8 Miller indices and interplanar spacing

Miller indices encode the orientation of a family of parallel lattice planes. Find the intercepts of a plane on the a,b,ca,b,ca,b,c axes in lattice units, take reciprocals, and clear fractions. An infinite intercept gives reciprocal zero; a negative intercept is written with a bar.

  • Intercepts (a,∞,∞)(a,\infty,\infty)(a,∞,∞) give (100)(100)(100).
  • Intercepts (a,b,∞)(a,b,\infty)(a,b,∞) give (110)(110)(110).
  • Intercepts (a,b,c)(a,b,c)(a,b,c) give (111)(111)(111).
  • A plane through the origin is replaced by a parallel plane before taking intercepts.
Derivation · Cubic interplanar spacing
∣Ghkl∣=2πah2+k2+l2|\mathbf G_{hkl}|=\frac{2\pi}{a}\sqrt{h^2+k^2+l^2}∣Ghkl​∣=a2π​h2+k2+l2​

The reciprocal-lattice vector is normal to the (hkl)(hkl)(hkl) planes.

dhkl=2π∣Ghkl∣d_{hkl}=\frac{2\pi}{|\mathbf G_{hkl}|}dhkl​=∣Ghkl​∣2π​

Adjacent planes differ in phase by one full reciprocal period.

Result
dhkl=ah2+k2+l2d_{hkl}=\frac{a}{\sqrt{h^2+k^2+l^2}}dhkl​=h2+k2+l2​a​

2.9 Bragg diffraction and systematic absences

X-ray wavelengths are comparable with interatomic spacings. Waves scattered from successive parallel planes interfere constructively when their path difference is an integral multiple of the wavelength.

Derivation · Bragg's law
path difference=2dsin⁡θ\text{path difference}=2d\sin\thetapath difference=2dsinθ

One ray travels an additional distance dsin⁡θd\sin\thetadsinθ on entering and another dsin⁡θd\sin\thetadsinθ on leaving.

2dsin⁡θ=nλ2d\sin\theta=n\lambda2dsinθ=nλ

Constructive interference requires an integral number of wavelengths.

Result
nλ=2dhklsin⁡θn\lambda=2d_{hkl}\sin\thetanλ=2dhkl​sinθ

Powder diffraction contains many randomly oriented crystallites, so some crystallites satisfy the Bragg condition for each allowed plane family. Peak positions reveal ddd spacings; peak intensities depend on the basis and atomic scattering factors.

Monatomic cubic latticeAllowed reflections
Primitive cubicAll integer hklhklhkl
BCCh+k+lh+k+lh+k+l even
FCCh,k,lh,k,lh,k,l all even or all odd
Selection rules assume an identical monatomic basis

Adding different atoms to the basis changes the structure factor. The simple BCC/FCC extinction rules must not be applied blindly to ordered binary structures.

6
Worked example

Index a BCC reflection

Which of (100)(100)(100), (110)(110)(110), (111)(111)(111) and (200)(200)(200) are allowed for a monatomic BCC lattice?

  1. Apply h+k+lh+k+lh+k+l even.
  2. (100)(100)(100): 1, forbidden; (110)(110)(110): 2, allowed.
  3. (111)(111)(111): 3, forbidden; (200)(200)(200): 2, allowed.
The allowed reflections are (110)(110)(110) and (200)(200)(200).

Cubic unit cells: counting, contact and packing

Three arrangements of identical spheres in a cube cover most metals. Build each one, slice it to see what belongs to the cell, then derive its packing efficiency from the geometry.

A unit cell is the smallest block that builds the whole crystal when repeated by translation in three directions. Atoms on the boundary of the cell are shared with neighbouring cells, so the cell owns only a fraction of each. The fraction depends on how many cells meet there:

18\tfrac1881​

14\tfrac1441​

4 cells meet
12\tfrac1221​
Face centre
2 cells meet
111
Body centre
inside the cell

The number of atoms owned by a cell is Z (also called the effective number of atoms). Z = (corners × ⅛) + (edge centres × ¼) + (faces × ½) + (body atoms × 1).

Given

To find

    dface=4rd_{\text{face}} = 4rdface​=4r(1)
  2. 2

  3. 3

    2 a=4r  ⇒  a=22 r\sqrt2\,a = 4r \;\Rightarrow\; a = 2\sqrt2\,r2​a=4r⇒a=22​r(3)
  4. 4

    Z=8×18+6×12=4Z = 8\times\tfrac18 + 6\times\tfrac12 = 4Z=8×81​+6×21​=4(4)

    η=4⋅43πr3(22 r)3=163πr3162 r3\eta = \frac{4\cdot\tfrac43\pi r^3}{(2\sqrt2\,r)^3} = \frac{\tfrac{16}{3}\pi r^3}{16\sqrt2\,r^3}η=(22​r)34⋅34​πr3​=162​r3316​πr3​(5)

η=π32=0.740  (74.0%)\eta = \dfrac{\pi}{3\sqrt2} = 0.740\;(74.0\%)η=32​π​=0.740(74.0%)∎
Walk through step by step
Why the contact line differs
In a simple cube the corner atoms are close enough to touch along the edge. In BCC the body-centre atom pushes the corner atoms apart, so contact moves to the body diagonal. In FCC the face-centre atoms do the same along the face diagonal. The contact line sets how the edge a depends on the radius r, and from that every other number follows.
JEE traps
  • FCC shows 14 atoms but Z = 4; BCC shows 9 but Z = 2. Z counts what the cell owns, not what you can see.
  • Packing efficiency order: SC (52.4%) < BCC (68.0%) < FCC (74.0%). HCP equals FCC.
  • In BCC the corner atoms do not touch each other; in FCC the corner atoms do not touch each other either. Contact is always between a corner and the centring atom.

Neighbour shells and coordination number

The coordination number is the number of nearest neighbours. Beyond them sit more shells at larger distances. Step through the shells: the counts and distances below come straight from the lattice, not from a table.

Computed by listing every lattice point around one atom and grouping them by distance. Nearest shells: SC 6, BCC 8, FCC 12. In BCC the 6 next-nearest atoms are only 15% farther than the 8 nearest, which is why it is sometimes called 8 + 6 coordinated.

Density of a crystal

The mass in one cell is Z·M / N_A and its volume is a³. So the density of the crystal is fixed by the lattice and the edge length, and a measured density lets you find Z, M or N_A.

Planes, Miller indices and X-ray diffraction

A crystal can be sliced into sets of parallel, equally spaced lattice planes. A plane is named by its Miller indices (hkl)(hkl)(hkl): take the intercepts on the three axes in units of the cell edge, invert them, and clear fractions. A plane parallel to an axis meets it at infinity, so its index is 000. Negative intercepts are written with a bar over the index.

Derivation 2.4

Spacing of the (hkl) planes in a cubic lattice

Given
A cubic lattice of edge aaa. The plane nearest the origin in the family (hkl)(hkl)(hkl) has intercepts a/ha/ha/h, a/ka/ka/k, a/la/la/l on the three axes.
To find
The perpendicular distance dhkld_{hkl}dhkl​ between neighbouring planes of the family.
  1. 1
    The plane hx+ky+lz=ahx + ky + lz = ahx+ky+lz=a passes through the three intercepts. Its unit normal points along (h,k,l)(h,k,l)(h,k,l):
    n^=(h, k, l)h2+k2+l2\hat n = \frac{(h,\,k,\,l)}{\sqrt{h^2+k^2+l^2}}n^=h2+k2+l2​(h,k,l)​(1)
  2. 2
    Planes of the family are equally spaced, and the plane nearest the origin lies at distance ddd from it. That distance is the projection of any point on the plane, for example the intercept (a/h, 0, 0)(a/h,\,0,\,0)(a/h,0,0), on the unit normal:
    dhkl=ah n^x=ah⋅hh2+k2+l2d_{hkl} = \frac{a}{h}\,\hat n_x = \frac{a}{h}\cdot\frac{h}{\sqrt{h^2+k^2+l^2}}dhkl​=ha​n^x​=ha​⋅h2+k2+l2​h​(2)
  3. 3
    The index hhh cancels, and the same result follows from the other two intercepts.
Hence
dhkl=ah2+k2+l2d_{hkl} = \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{h^2+k^2+l^2}}dhkl​=h2+k2+l2​a​∎

For example d100=ad_{100} = ad100​=a, d110=a/2d_{110} = a/\sqrt2d110​=a/2​ and d111=a/3d_{111} = a/\sqrt3d111​=a/3​. The densest planes are the most widely spaced.

Walk through step by step
Derivation 2.5

Bragg's law

Given
A beam of X-rays of wavelength λ\lambdaλ falls at glancing angle θ\thetaθ on a family of parallel planes a distance ddd apart. Each plane reflects specularly.
To find
The condition under which the reflections from all the planes reinforce one another.
  1. 1
    Take two rays. Ray 1 reflects at the point PPP on the upper plane; ray 2 reflects at the point QQQ on the next plane, directly below PPP, so PQ=dPQ = dPQ=d.
  2. 2
    Drop perpendiculars from PPP onto the incoming and outgoing paths of ray 2, meeting them at AAA and CCC. Up to AAA and from CCC onward the two rays have travelled equal distances, so the extra path of ray 2 is AQ+QCAQ + QCAQ+QC.
  3. 3
    In the right triangle PAQPAQPAQ the angle at QQQ between QPQPQP and the ray is 90∘−θ90^\circ - \theta90∘−θ, because the ray makes θ\thetaθ with the plane and PQPQPQ is normal to it. Hence:
    AQ=PQcos⁡(90∘−θ)=dsin⁡θ,QC=dsin⁡θAQ = PQ\cos(90^\circ - \theta) = d\sin\theta, \qquad QC = d\sin\thetaAQ=PQcos(90∘−θ)=dsinθ,QC=dsinθ(1)
  4. 4
    Add the two segments to get the path difference:
    δ=AQ+QC=2dsin⁡θ\delta = AQ + QC = 2d\sin\thetaδ=AQ+QC=2dsinθ(2)
  5. 5
    The rays leave in step, and the reflections reinforce, only if the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths:
    δ=nλ,n=1,2,3,…\delta = n\lambda, \quad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldotsδ=nλ,n=1,2,3,…(3)
Hence
nλ=2dsin⁡θn\lambda = 2d\sin\thetanλ=2dsinθ∎

Since sin⁡θ≤1\sin\theta \le 1sinθ≤1, reflections are possible only when λ≤2d\lambda \le 2dλ≤2d. The wavelength must be comparable to the atomic spacing, which is why X-rays are used.

Walk through step by step

Try it. At the starting values the path difference is exactly one wavelength. Slide the angle and the spacing and watch the reflected intensity rise and fall.

Constructive. The path difference is 2dsin⁡θ=1542d\sin\theta = 1542dsinθ=154 pm =1λ= 1\lambda=1λ, a whole number of wavelengths, so the reflections from successive planes add up.

Which planes actually reflect?
The lattice type removes some reflections: waves from the extra centring atoms arrive exactly out of step. In a simple cubic lattice every (hkl)(hkl)(hkl) appears. In BCC only reflections with h+k+lh+k+lh+k+l even appear. In FCC only those with h,k,lh,k,lh,k,l all odd or all even appear. Counting the allowed lines in a powder pattern therefore tells you the lattice type.

Empty space along an edge, and formulas from positions

Atoms that do not touch along the cell edge leave a gap there. The gap, as a fraction of the edge, is a favourite exam quantity. It also gives a quick route from a measured gap to the edge length, and so to the density.

Derivation 2.6

Fraction of the cell edge left unoccupied

Given
Identical atoms of radius rrr in a cubic cell of edge aaa, touching along the contact line found in derivations 2.1 to 2.3.
To find
The fraction (a−2r)/a(a - 2r)/a(a−2r)/a of an edge that no atom covers.
  1. 1
    Simple cubic. Contact is along the edge, a=2ra = 2ra=2r, so nothing is left over:
    a−2ra=0\frac{a - 2r}{a} = 0aa−2r​=0(1)
  2. 2
    BCC. Contact is along the body diagonal, r=34ar = \dfrac{\sqrt3}{4}ar=43​​a. Two corner atoms on an edge take up 2r=32a2r = \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}a2r=23​​a:
    a−2ra=1−32=0.134\frac{a - 2r}{a} = 1 - \frac{\sqrt3}{2} = 0.134aa−2r​=1−23​​=0.134(2)
  3. 3
    FCC. Contact is along the face diagonal, r=24ar = \dfrac{\sqrt2}{4}ar=42​​a, so 2r=a22r = \dfrac{a}{\sqrt2}2r=2​a​:
    a−2ra=1−12=0.293\frac{a - 2r}{a} = 1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt2} = 0.293aa−2r​=1−2​1​=0.293(3)
Hence
SC: 0,BCC: 0.134 a,FCC: 0.293 a\text{SC: } 0,\qquad \text{BCC: } 0.134\,a,\qquad \text{FCC: } 0.293\,aSC: 0,BCC: 0.134a,FCC: 0.293a∎

The gap between the inner surfaces of two corner atoms on an edge is therefore 0.134 a0.134\,a0.134a in BCC and 0.293 a0.293\,a0.293a in FCC.

Here ZZZ denotes the number of atoms per conventional unit cell for a monatomic crystal. In an ionic crystal, ZZZ usually denotes formula units per cell and must be obtained by counting each species.

Do not transfer monatomic $Z$ blindly

The geometry ‘FCC’ tells you the number of lattice points in the conventional cell. The number of chemical formula units depends on the basis attached to those points.

3.2 Contact directions and radius–edge relations

In the equal-sphere model, the line joining centres of touching spheres determines the relation between atomic radius rrr and cube edge aaa.

Derivation · Simple cubic
a=2ra=2ra=2r

Nearest corner atoms touch along a cube edge.

Result
r=a2r=\frac{a}{2}r=2a​

body diagonal=3a\text{body diagonal}=\sqrt3abody diagonal=3​a

3a=4r\sqrt3a=4r3​a=4r

Four radii span the complete body diagonal.

Result
r=34ar=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}ar=43​​a
Derivation · Face-centred cubic
face diagonal=2a\text{face diagonal}=\sqrt2aface diagonal=2​a

A face diagonal passes through corner–face centre–corner.

2a=4r\sqrt2a=4r2​a=4r

Four radii span the complete face diagonal.

Result
r=a22r=\frac{a}{2\sqrt2}r=22​a​

Worked example

Atomic radius from density-independent geometry

Copper is treated as FCC with a=361.5 pma=361.5\ \mathrm{pm}a=361.5 pm. Calculate its metallic radius.

  1. For FCC, r=a/(22)r=a/(2\sqrt2)r=a/(22​).
  2. r=361.5/(22)=127.8 pmr=361.5/(2\sqrt2)=127.8\ \mathrm{pm}r=361.5/(22​)=127.8 pm.
The metallic radius is approximately 128 pm128\ \mathrm{pm}128 pm.

3.3 Coordination number and neighbour shells

The coordination number of an atom in a monatomic crystal is the number of nearest neighbours at the shortest centre-to-centre distance. Successive neighbour shells occur at larger discrete distances.

LatticeFirst shellSecond shellThird shell
SC6 at aaa12 at 2a\sqrt2a2​a8 at 3a\sqrt3a3​a
BCC8 at 3a/2\sqrt3a/23​a/26 at aaa12 at 2a\sqrt2a2​a
FCC12 at a/2a/\sqrt2a/2​6 at aaa24 at a3/2a\sqrt{3/2}a3/2​

The FCC and HCP lattices both have coordination number 12 and the same maximum packing fraction, but they differ in the stacking sequence of close-packed layers.

2
Worked example

Nearest-neighbour distance in BCC

A BCC metal has edge length a=300 pma=300\ \mathrm{pm}a=300 pm. Find its nearest-neighbour distance.

  1. A corner atom's nearest neighbours are body-centre atoms in adjacent cells.
  2. The distance is half a body diagonal: d=3a/2d=\sqrt3a/2d=3​a/2.
  3. d=259.8 pmd=259.8\ \mathrm{pm}d=259.8 pm.
The nearest-neighbour distance is about 260 pm260\ \mathrm{pm}260 pm.

Derivation · General density expression
mcell=ZMNAm_{cell}=\frac{ZM}{N_A}mcell​=NA​ZM​

A cell containing ZZZ formula units has this mass.

ρ=mcellVcell\rho=\frac{m_{cell}}{V_{cell}}ρ=Vcell​mcell​​

Density is mass divided by cell volume.

Result
ρ=ZMNAVcell\rho=\frac{ZM}{N_AV_{cell}}ρ=NA​Vcell​ZM​

For a cubic cell, Vcell=a3V_{cell}=a^3Vcell​=a3. Use consistent units: if aaa is in centimetres and MMM in grams per mole, ρ\rhoρ is obtained in g cm−3\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}gcm−3.

ρ=ZMNAa3\rho=\frac{ZM}{N_Aa^3}ρ=NA​a3ZM​

Worked example

Identify a cubic lattice from density

A metal of molar mass 55.85 g mol−155.85\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}55.85 gmol−1 has a=286.7 pma=286.7\ \mathrm{pm}a=286.7 pm and density 7.87 g cm−37.87\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}7.87 gcm−3. Estimate ZZZ.

  1. Convert aaa: 286.7 pm=2.867×10−8 cm286.7\ \mathrm{pm}=2.867\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm}286.7 pm=2.867×10−8 cm.
  2. Use Z=ρNAa3/MZ=\rho N_Aa^3/MZ=ρNA​a3/M.
  3. Substitution gives Z≈2.00Z\approx2.00Z≈2.00.
The conventional cell contains two atoms; the metal is consistent with BCC.
Experimental density can reveal defects

If the measured density differs from the ideal value, vacancies, interstitials, impurities, porosity or a wrong structural assignment may be responsible.

3.5 Formula determination from fractional occupancy

Count every species independently. Site occupancy means the fraction of a set of crystallographically equivalent sites that is actually occupied.

NX=∑snsfsqsN_X=\sum_s n_s f_s q_sNX​=s∑​ns​fs​qs​

For species X, nsn_sns​ is the number of sites of type sss per cell, fsf_sfs​ the boundary contribution and qsq_sqs​ the occupancy fraction.

4
Worked example

Occupancy problem

A cubic cell has A on all corners, B on all face centres, and C on one-half of the twelve edge centres. Determine the formula.

  1. A: 8(1/8)=18(1/8)=18(1/8)=1.
  2. B: 6(1/2)=36(1/2)=36(1/2)=3.
  3. C: 12(1/4)(1/2)=3/212(1/4)(1/2)=3/212(1/4)(1/2)=3/2.
  4. Ratio 1:3:1.51:3:1.51:3:1.5; multiply by 2.
The empirical formula is A2B6C3\mathrm{A_2B_6C_3}A2​B6​C3​.

3.6 Atom-removal and surface-counting problems

When a geometric operation removes atoms from a finite conventional cell, count only the fractions originally belonging to that cell. A line or plane can include corners, edge centres, face centres and internal sites.

5
Worked example

Removing an FCC face

All atoms lying on one complete face of an FCC conventional cell are removed from that cell. What is the decrease in the atom count assigned to the cell?

  1. The chosen face has four corner atoms, each contributing 1/81/81/8 to the selected three-dimensional cell.
  2. It has one face-centre atom contributing 1/21/21/2.
  3. Decrease =4(1/8)+1/2=1=4(1/8)+1/2=1=4(1/8)+1/2=1.
The cell's assigned atom count decreases by 1, from 4 to 3.
Finite object versus periodic crystal

Removing one face from a drawn cell is a bookkeeping exercise. In an infinite periodic lattice, the same boundary sites are shared with neighbouring cells, so the physical operation must be defined carefully.

3.7 Surface gaps and coordinate-tracking algorithm

In BCC, corner atoms do not touch along an edge. The centre-to-centre edge separation is aaa, while each sphere has diameter 2r=3a/22r=\sqrt3a/22r=3​a/2. The surface gap is therefore positive.

gedge=a−2r=a(1−32)g_{edge}=a-2r=a\left(1-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)gedge​=a−2r=a(1−23​​)

For atom-removal problems, first write the fractional coordinates of every occupied site on the specified line or plane. Then subtract only the contribution that each removed boundary site originally made to the selected conventional cell.

  • Identify the geometric object: edge, face diagonal, body diagonal or plane.
  • List occupied coordinates lying exactly on it.
  • Apply corner/edge/face/internal sharing fractions.
  • Subtract species separately and reduce the final ratio.
6
Worked example

Remove one face diagonal

A cell has A at all corners, B at all face centres and C at the body centre. Remove the sites lying on one face diagonal. Find the remaining A:B:C ratio.

  1. Initially A=1, B=3, C=1.
  2. The chosen face diagonal contains two corner A sites and one face-centre B site.
  3. Remaining A =1−2(1/8)=3/4=1-2(1/8)=3/4=1−2(1/8)=3/4; B =3−1/2=5/2=3-1/2=5/2=3−1/2=5/2; C =1=1=1.
  4. Multiply by 4.
The remaining ratio is A:B:C =3:10:4=3:10:4=3:10:4.

Close packing, voids and diamond

Metals and many ionic lattices are built by stacking layers of spheres as tightly as possible. The gaps left between layers, the voids, are where smaller ions sit.

Packing in one plane

Before stacking in three dimensions, see how circles pack in a plane. Squares waste more area; shifting alternate rows into the dips of the previous row packs them as tightly as possible.

Voids in the HCP cell

Think of oranges stacked in a shop. Between the oranges there are gaps. A hole is one of those gaps. There are only two shapes of gap.

Small hole = tetrahedral void (T.V.)
A small gap with 4 balls around it: 3 touching on one side and 1 on the other, like the corners of a tiny pyramid. A ball that fits in it can be at most 0.225 times the size of the big balls.
Big hole = octahedral void (O.V.)
A bigger gap with 6 balls around it: 3 below and 3 above, twisted against each other, like two pyramids stuck base to base. A ball that fits in it can be up to 0.414 times the size of the big balls.

Rule to remember: for every 1 ball there are 2 small holes and 1 big hole. The hexagonal box (unit cell) has 6 balls, so it has 12 small holes and 6 big holes. Walk up the box floor by floor and count them yourself.

JEE traps
  • For N close-packed atoms there are N octahedral and 2N tetrahedral voids, in both HCP and CCP.

4.1 Packing fraction and empty space

Packing fraction is the fraction of cell volume occupied by hard spheres. Packing efficiency is the same quantity expressed as a percentage; void fraction is the unoccupied remainder.

η=Z(43πr3)Vcell\eta=\frac{Z\left(\frac43\pi r^3\right)}{V_{cell}}η=Vcell​Z(34​πr3)​
% empty=100(1−η)\%\,empty=100(1-\eta)%empty=100(1−η)
Hard-sphere model

Packing fractions compare geometrical models. Electron density is not bounded by a sharp classical sphere, so the model is structural rather than a literal map of all occupied space.

4.2 One- and two-dimensional packing

In one dimension, each sphere touches two neighbours and the coordination number is 2. In two dimensions, equal circles form either a square arrangement or a triangular (hexagonal) arrangement.

The depressions in a triangular layer form two alternating sets, commonly labelled B and C. A second layer can occupy one set, leading to close-packed three-dimensional stacking.

BCC is denser than SC but is not a close-packed structure. No plane in the BCC lattice has the triangular arrangement that characterises close packing.

4.5 Close-packed layers: HCP and CCP

Begin with a triangular A layer. A second layer placed in one set of triangular depressions is B. For the third layer there are two choices: place it above A to form ABAB… hexagonal close packing, or occupy the remaining C depressions to form ABCABC… cubic close packing.

StackingStructureConventional descriptionCoordination number
AAA…Simple hexagonalLayers directly eclipsed8 in ideal equal-sphere simple hexagonal packing
ABAB…HCPHexagonal unit cell12
ABCABC…CCP = FCCCubic F-centred cell12
Derivation · FCC/CCP packing efficiency
Z=4Z=4Z=4

Four atoms belong to the FCC conventional cell.

a=22ra=2\sqrt2ra=22​r

Contact occurs along a face diagonal.

η=4(43πr3)(22r)3\eta=\frac{4(\frac43\pi r^3)}{(2\sqrt2r)^3}η=(22​r)34(34​πr3)​

Substitute and simplify.

Result
ηFCC=π32=0.7405\eta_{FCC}=\frac{\pi}{3\sqrt2}=0.7405ηFCC​=32​π​=0.7405

HCP and CCP have the same local coordination and packing efficiency because both are built from identical close-packed layers. Their difference first appears in the third layer and affects longer-range symmetry.

2
Worked example

Stacking identification

A close-packed solid has layer sequence ABACABAC…. Is it ideal HCP or ideal CCP?

  1. Ideal HCP repeats every two layers as ABAB….
  2. Ideal CCP repeats every three layers as ABCABC….
  3. ABAC has a four-layer repeat and contains stacking faults relative to both ideals.
It is neither perfect HCP nor perfect CCP; it is a faulted/polytypic close-packed sequence.

c=2htet=4r23c=2h_{tet}=4r\sqrt{\frac23}c=2htet​=4r32​​

The conventional HCP cell spans A–B–A.

a=2ra=2ra=2r

Spheres touch within a basal layer.

Result
ca=83=1.633\frac{c}{a}=\sqrt{\frac83}=1.633ac​=38​​=1.633

Maximum equal-sphere packing

Kepler's theorem establishes that no arrangement of congruent spheres in three-dimensional Euclidean space exceeds the HCP/CCP density π/(32)\pi/(3\sqrt2)π/(32​).

4.8 Polytypes, stacking faults and eutactic arrays

Close-packed layer notation extends beyond ideal HCP and CCP. Longer periodic sequences such as ABAC, ABCACB or mixed cubic–hexagonal sequences are polytypes: they have the same composition and closely related local coordination but differ in stacking order.

SequenceDescription
ABAB…Ideal hexagonal close packing
ABCABC…Ideal cubic close packing
ABAC…Four-layer polytype
Local repetition errorStacking fault

In many ionic structures, the larger anions preserve the topology of a close-packed array but are pushed apart by cations. Such an arrangement is often called eutactic rather than strictly close packed, because the anions need not remain in mutual contact.

Local versus long-range identity

HCP and CCP have identical first-neighbour coordination. Diffraction or longer-range layer tracing is needed to distinguish their stacking.

5.1 Meaning of a void

A void is an interstitial region enclosed by neighbouring packed particles. It is not an empty lattice point in the Bravais sense. The size and coordination of a void depend on the geometry of the surrounding spheres.

VoidNumber of surrounding spheresCoordination geometry
Triangular void3Planar triangle
Tetrahedral void4Tetrahedron
Octahedral void6Octahedron
Cubic void8Cube
Void count is tied to packed-particle count

For a close-packed array containing NNN host particles, there are NNN octahedral and 2N2N2N tetrahedral holes. This statement is independent of whether the close packing is HCP or CCP.

5.2 Formation of tetrahedral and octahedral holes

When a B-layer sphere covers a triangular depression in an A layer, the enclosed region between the three A spheres and one B sphere is a tetrahedral hole. When an upward triangular depression in one layer lies opposite a downward depression in the next, six spheres enclose an octahedral hole.

Ntet=2N,Noct=NN_{tet}=2N,\qquad N_{oct}=NNtet​=2N,Noct​=N
Derivation · Void count from one close-packed layer
triangular depressions=2N\text{triangular depressions}=2Ntriangular depressions=2N

A large triangular layer of NNN spheres has approximately 2N2N2N triangular depressions, boundary effects neglected.

N depressions are covered by the next layerN\text{ depressions are covered by the next layer}N depressions are covered by the next layer

Each covered depression produces one tetrahedral hole on that side.

N opposite pairs form octahedral holes across layersN\text{ opposite pairs form octahedral holes across layers}N opposite pairs form octahedral holes across layers

Layer stacking gives the final 2:1 tetrahedral-to-octahedral count.

Result
Ntet:Noct=2:1N_{tet}:N_{oct}=2:1Ntet​:Noct​=2:1

Hole counting

A close-packed anion array contains 240 anions. How many tetrahedral and octahedral holes are available?

  1. Tetrahedral holes =2N=480=2N=480=2N=480.
  2. Octahedral holes =N=240=N=240=N=240.
There are 480 tetrahedral and 240 octahedral holes.

An FCC conventional cell contains four host particles. Hence it contains four octahedral holes and eight tetrahedral holes in total.

Worked example

Mixed-hole occupancy

Anions are close packed. Cations occupy one-quarter of tetrahedral holes and one-half of octahedral holes. Determine the formula.

  1. Cation/anion =2(1/4)+(1/2)=1=2(1/4)+(1/2)=1=2(1/4)+(1/2)=1.
  2. Thus cation and anion numbers are equal.
The ideal formula is MX.

5.5 Sizes of interstitial holes

The largest sphere that fits a hole while touching all host spheres has a limiting radius. For host radius RRR and interstitial radius rrr, the classical values follow from regular polyhedral geometry.

HoleLimiting r/Rr/Rr/RDerivation result
Triangular0.1552/3−12/\sqrt3-12/3​−1
Tetrahedral0.2253/2−1\sqrt{3/2}-13/2​−1
Octahedral0.4142−1\sqrt2-12​−1
Cubic0.7323−1\sqrt3-13​−1

These are geometrical lower limits for a cation to maintain contact with surrounding anions without forcing them apart. They are not exact universal boundaries for real ionic compounds.

Distortion and covalency

Polarisation, directional covalent bonding, unequal compressibility and temperature can stabilise a coordination number outside the simple radius-ratio prediction.

5.6 Diamond structure

Diamond can be described as an FCC lattice with the basis (0,0,0)(0,0,0)(0,0,0) and (1/4,1/4,1/4)(1/4,1/4,1/4)(1/4,1/4,1/4). Equivalently, one carbon sublattice is displaced from another by one-quarter of a body diagonal. Each carbon is tetrahedrally bonded to four neighbours.

5.7 Interstitial sites in the conventional HCP cell

The conventional HCP prism contains six host atoms. The universal close-packing rule therefore gives twelve tetrahedral and six octahedral holes. These sites occur in alternating planes between the lower A, middle B and upper A layers.

Ntet=2(6)=12,Noct=6N_{tet}=2(6)=12,\qquad N_{oct}=6Ntet​=2(6)=12,Noct​=6

Layer-by-layer sketches often mark interstitial planes at fractional heights such as h/8h/8h/8, 2h/82h/82h/8, 3h/83h/83h/8 and so on. Those labels are a visual bookkeeping device; the invariant result is the total count and coordination of the holes.

5
Worked example

HCP hole occupancy

An HCP anion cell contains six anions. If one-third of its octahedral holes and one-quarter of its tetrahedral holes are occupied, how many cations belong to the cell?

  1. Octahedral cations =(1/3)(6)=2=(1/3)(6)=2=(1/3)(6)=2.
  2. Tetrahedral cations =(1/4)(12)=3=(1/4)(12)=3=(1/4)(12)=3.
  3. Total cations =5=5=5.
The cell contains 5 cations for 6 anions.

PART 4

Ionic crystals and the radius-ratio rule

Ions pack so that each is surrounded by as many oppositely charged neighbours as it can touch. The ratio of their radii decides how many that is, and therefore which structure forms.

In an ionic crystal the larger ions (usually anions) form the framework and the smaller ions sit in its voids. A small cation that touches too few anions rattles; a large cation that does not fit pushes the anions apart. The best fit is when the cation just touches all its neighbours while the anions just touch each other. That fixes a limiting radius ratio for each coordination geometry.

Derivation 4.3

Coordination number 4 (tetrahedral)

Given
A cation of radius r+r_+r+​ surrounded by 4 anions of radius r−r_-r−​. The anions touch the cation, and in the limiting case they also touch one another.
To find
The limiting radius ratio r+/r−r_+/r_-r+​/r−​ at which this arrangement is just stable.
  1. 1
    Put the four anions on alternate corners of a cube of edge bbb and the cation at the cube's centre. Anions touch along face diagonals:
    2 b=2r−\sqrt2\,b = 2r_-2​b=2r−​(1)
  2. 2
    The cation touches each anion along half of a body diagonal:
    r++r−=32 br_+ + r_- = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\,br+​+r−​=23​​b(2)
  3. 3
    Substitute b=2 r−b = \sqrt2\,r_-b=2​r−​:
    r++r−=322 r−=32 r−r_+ + r_- = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\sqrt2\,r_- = \sqrt{\tfrac32}\,r_-r+​+r−​=23​​2​r−​=23​​r−​(3)
Hence
r+r−=32−1=0.225\dfrac{r_+}{r_-} = \sqrt{\tfrac32} - 1 = 0.225r−​r+​​=23​​−1=0.225∎
Walk through step by step
Radius ratio r₊/r₋Coordination no.GeometryExample
below 0.1552LinearCO₂ (molecular), Cu₂O around Cu⁺
0.155 – 0.2253Trigonal planarB₂O₃
0.225 – 0.4144TetrahedralZnS

How to use the table
Compute r₊/r₋ (small over large) and read off the coordination number. NaCl: 95/181 = 0.52, so CN 6. CsCl: 169/181 = 0.93, so CN 8. ZnS: 74/184 = 0.40, so CN 4. The rule predicts the right structure for most simple ionic solids; it is a guide, not a law.

Beyond eight: larger coordination numbers

The same geometry, applied to higher coordination, gives the lower limits below. Ionic crystals rarely go past 8, but complex ions, intermetallics and the close-packed metals reach 12.

Geometry around the cationCNLower limit of r₊/r₋
Linear2—
Trigonal planar30.155
Tetrahedral40.225
Octahedral60.414
Trigonal prism60.528
Pentagonal bipyramid70.592
Cube80.732
Dodecahedron (square antiprism)80.668
Icosahedron120.902
Cuboctahedron121.000
Temperature and pressure change the coordination number
Pressure squeezes ions closer, so the structure with the higher coordination number is favoured: NaCl (6 : 6) turns into the CsCl type (8 : 8) at very high pressure, about 30 GPa. Heating expands the lattice and favours the lower coordination number: CsCl (8 : 8) changes to the NaCl type (6 : 6) at about 445 °C.
If nothing is given, assume the ideal crystal
An ideal crystal is one in which the cation just touches the anions and the anions just touch each other, so the radius ratio sits at the limiting value for its coordination number: 0.414 for NaCl and 0.732 for CsCl. When r+/r−r_+/r_-r+​/r−​ is smaller than the limit the anions touch each other and the cation rattles; the edge is then fixed by the anions alone.
Derivation 4.7

Packing efficiency of an ideal rock-salt crystal

Given
An ideal NaCl-type crystal: the anions form an FCC lattice and just touch along the face diagonal, while each cation just fits the octahedral void, so r+/r−=0.414r_+/r_- = 0.414r+​/r−​=0.414.
To find
The fraction of the cell volume occupied by the ions.
  1. 1
    The anions touch along the face diagonal, which carries four anion radii:
    2 a=4r−;⇒;a=22 r−\sqrt2\,a = 4r_- ;\Rightarrow; a = 2\sqrt2\,r_-2​a=4r−​;⇒;a=22​r−​(1)
  2. 2
    Ions per cell: 4 anions (FCC) and 4 cations (octahedral voids), so Z=4Z = 4Z=4 formula units. The ideal radius ratio gives r+=0.414 r−r_+ = 0.414\,r_-r+​=0.414r−​, and:
    Vions=4⋅43π(r−3+r+3)=163π r−3 (1+0.4143)V_{\text{ions}} = 4\cdot\tfrac43\pi\left(r_-^3 + r_+^3\right) = \tfrac{16}{3}\pi\,r_-^3\,(1 + 0.414^3)Vions​=4⋅34​π(r−3​+r+3​)=316​πr−3​(1+0.4143)(2)
  3. 3
    Volume of the cell:
    Vcell=a3=(22 r−)3=22.63 r−3V_{\text{cell}} = a^3 = (2\sqrt2\,r_-)^3 = 22.63\,r_-^3Vcell​=a3=(22​r−​)3=22.63r−3​(3)
  4. 4
    Divide, using 1+0.4143=1.0711 + 0.414^3 = 1.0711+0.4143=1.071:
    η=16.755×1.07122.63=0.793\eta = \frac{16.755 \times 1.071}{22.63} = 0.793η=22.6316.755×1.071​=0.793(4)
Hence
η≈0.79  (79%)\eta \approx 0.79\;(79\%)η≈0.79(79%)∎

This is the largest possible packing efficiency of a rock-salt crystal. Any real NaCl-type crystal with r+/r−>0.414r_+/r_- > 0.414r+​/r−​>0.414 has a larger cation, the anions are pushed apart, and the efficiency is lower.

Derivation 4.6

Cell edge from the ionic radii

Given
Ions are hard spheres. In each structure the cation and anion touch along a definite line of the cell, and the ionic radii are r+r_+r+​ and r−r_-r−​.
To find
The edge aaa of the NaCl, CsCl and zinc blende cells in terms of r++r−r_+ + r_-r+​+r−​.
  1. 1

Walk through step by step
Corundum (Al₂O₃)
O²⁻ ions are hexagonally close packed. Al³⁺ fills two-thirds of the octahedral voids. For N oxide ions there are N octahedral voids, so Al = ⅔N, and Al : O = ⅔N : N = 2 : 3. Each Al³⁺ has coordination 6 and each O²⁻ has 4.
JEE traps
  • In fluorite (CaF₂) the cation coordination is 8 and the anion's is 4. In anti-fluorite (Li₂O) they are exchanged: 4 and 8.
  • CsCl is not body-centred cubic: the centre ion differs from the corner ions, so the lattice is simple cubic with a two-ion basis.
  • Zinc blende and wurtzite are both 4 : 4. They differ in the stacking of the anion layers (ABC against AB).
  • In an FCC arrangement of N anions, filling all tetrahedral voids gives 2N cations (M₂X), and filling half gives N (MX).

6.1 Purpose of the radius-ratio model

For an ionic solid approximated by rigid spheres, the cation-to-anion radius ratio r+/r−r_+/r_-r+​/r−​ indicates whether a cation can fit a particular hole while maintaining contact with surrounding anions. At the limiting ratio, the anions just touch one another and the cation simultaneously touches every coordinating anion.

λ=r+r−\lambda=\frac{r_+}{r_-}λ=r−​r+​​

If λ\lambdaλ falls below a critical value for a proposed geometry, the cation is too small to support that coordination shell in the undistorted hard-sphere model. The anions would collapse toward one another, favouring lower coordination.

6.2 Coordination number 3: triangular hole

Derivation · Triangular critical ratio
distance from triangle centre to vertex=2r−3\text{distance from triangle centre to vertex}=\frac{2r_-}{\sqrt3}distance from triangle centre to vertex=3​2r−​​

The equilateral-triangle side is 2r−2r_-2r−​.

r++r−=2r−3r_++r_-=\frac{2r_-}{\sqrt3}r+​+r−​=3​2r−​​

At the limit, the central cation touches all three anions.

Result
r+r−=23−1=0.1547\frac{r_+}{r_-}=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}-1=0.1547r−​r+​​=3​2​−1=0.1547

Ratios below 0.155 are commonly assigned coordination number 2; ratios from about 0.155 to 0.225 are associated with triangular coordination number 3 in the simplified chart.

6.3 Coordination number 4: tetrahedral hole

Derivation · Tetrahedral critical ratio
a=2r−a=2r_-a=2r−​

The four anions form a regular tetrahedron of edge aaa.

Rtet=64a=62r−R_{tet}=\frac{\sqrt6}{4}a=\frac{\sqrt6}{2}r_-Rtet​=46​​a=26​​r−​

The centre-to-vertex distance is the tetrahedral circumradius.

r++r−=Rtetr_++r_-=R_{tet}r+​+r−​=Rtet​

The cation touches all four anions.

Result
r+r−=32−1=0.2247\frac{r_+}{r_-}=\sqrt{\frac32}-1=0.2247r−​r+​​=23​​−1=0.2247

The usual radius-ratio interval for tetrahedral coordination is approximately 0.225≤r+/r−<0.4140.225\le r_+/r_-<0.4140.225≤r+​/r−​<0.414. Examples include Zn2+^{2+}2+ in zinc blende and Be2+^{2+}2+ in many tetrahedral environments.

Square-planar coordination

A square hole also has coordination number 4 but its limiting ratio is 2−1=0.414\sqrt2-1=0.4142​−1=0.414. Square-planar coordination is usually controlled by electronic structure and directional bonding rather than the elementary ionic radius-ratio chart.

6.4 Coordination number 6: octahedral hole

Derivation · Octahedral critical ratio
a=2r−a=2r_-a=2r−​

Four anions in an equatorial square touch along the square edges.

centre-to-corner distance=a2=2r−\text{centre-to-corner distance}=\frac{a}{\sqrt2}=\sqrt2r_-centre-to-corner distance=2​a​=2​r−​

This equals r++r−r_++r_-r+​+r−​.

Result
r+r−=2−1=0.4142\frac{r_+}{r_-}=\sqrt2-1=0.4142r−​r+​​=2​−1=0.4142

The classical octahedral range is 0.414≤r+/r−<0.7320.414\le r_+/r_-<0.7320.414≤r+​/r−​<0.732. Rock-salt structures place each ion in six-coordinate octahedral surroundings.

1
Worked example

Predicting a coordination number

Using the elementary radius-ratio rule, predict the likely coordination number for r+/r−=0.52r_+/r_-=0.52r+​/r−​=0.52.

  1. 0.52 is greater than the octahedral lower limit 0.414.
  2. It is less than the cubic lower limit 0.732.
The model predicts coordination number 6.

6.5 Coordination number 8: cubic hole

Derivation · Cubic critical ratio
a=2r−a=2r_-a=2r−​

Adjacent corner anions touch along a cube edge.

half body diagonal=3a2=3r−\text{half body diagonal}=\frac{\sqrt3a}{2}=\sqrt3r_-half body diagonal=23​a​=3​r−​

This is the centre-to-corner distance.

r++r−=3r−r_++r_-=\sqrt3r_-r+​+r−​=3​r−​

The central cation touches all eight anions.

Result
r+r−=3−1=0.7321\frac{r_+}{r_-}=\sqrt3-1=0.7321r−​r+​​=3​−1=0.7321

Ratios from about 0.732 to 1 are assigned coordination number 8 in the simple chart. CsCl-type structures are the standard example.

2
Worked example

Structure choice by ratio

Two MX salts have radius ratios 0.38 and 0.80. Which is geometrically more compatible with ZnS-type and CsCl-type coordination?

  1. 0.38 lies in the tetrahedral interval 0.225–0.414.
  2. 0.80 lies in the cubic interval 0.732–1.
The 0.38 salt is compatible with ZnS-type CN 4; the 0.80 salt with CsCl-type CN 8.

6.6 Radius-ratio summary

Radius ratio r+/r−r_+/r_-r+​/r−​Predicted CNIdeal geometryCommon structure association
0–0.1552LinearRare simple ionic solids
0.155–0.2253TriangularPlanar three-coordinate
0.225–0.4144TetrahedralZnS type
0.414–0.7326OctahedralNaCl type
0.732–1.0008CubicCsCl type
Boundary values

At an exact limiting value, two geometries can be geometrically competitive. Real structure selection depends on lattice energy, polarisation, covalency, pressure and temperature.

6.7 Why the rule is not absolute

  • Ionic radii depend on oxidation state, coordination number and the radius convention used.
  • Ions are not incompressible spheres; electron clouds deform and overlap.
  • Covalent character introduces directional bonding that the model omits.
  • The anion framework need not remain in mutual contact.
  • Pressure can stabilise higher coordination by favouring denser structures.
  • Lattice-energy differences involve the entire crystal, not only nearest-neighbour fit.

Use the radius-ratio rule as a first geometrical guide, not as a proof. When experimental structural data conflict with the chart, the structure is authoritative.

Connection with Fajans' rules

A small, highly charged cation can strongly polarise a large anion. Increased covalent character may favour coordination and geometry different from a rigid-sphere prediction.

6.8 Coordination polyhedra and connectivity

PolyhedronCNTypical sitePossible connections in extended solids
Tetrahedron4ZnS, silicatesCorner-, edge- or face-sharing
Octahedron6NaCl, rutile, perovskite B siteCorner-, edge- or face-sharing
Cube8CsCl, Ca site in fluoriteThree-dimensional cage
Cuboctahedron12Close-packed metals, perovskite A siteClose-packed coordination shell

The way polyhedra share corners, edges or faces affects cation–cation separation. For highly charged cations, face sharing often produces strong electrostatic repulsion and is less favourable than corner sharing, an idea related to Pauling's rules.

6.9 Coordination-number contact balance

In a binary structure Ax_xx​By_yy​, every A–B nearest-neighbour contact can be counted from either sublattice. Counting from A gives x CN(A)x\,\mathrm{CN}(A)xCN(A) contacts per formula set; counting from B gives y CN(B)y\,\mathrm{CN}(B)yCN(B). The two counts must be equal.

x CN(A)=y CN(B)x\,\mathrm{CN}(A)=y\,\mathrm{CN}(B)xCN(A)=yCN(B)
3
Worked example

Find the second coordination number

In A2_22​B3_33​, each A has six B nearest neighbours. Find the coordination number of B with respect to A.

  1. Use xCN(A)=yCN(B)x\mathrm{CN}(A)=y\mathrm{CN}(B)xCN(A)=yCN(B).
  2. 2×6=3CN(B)2\times6=3\mathrm{CN}(B)2×6=3CN(B).
CN(B)=4\mathrm{CN}(B)=4CN(B)=4.

6.10 Madelung energy and structural stability

Radius fit describes local geometry, but an ionic crystal is stabilised by Coulomb interactions with many shells. The dimensionless Madelung constant AAA summarises the geometry of the infinite electrostatic sum for a chosen structure type.

UCoul=−NAAz+z−e24πε0r0U_{Coul}=-\frac{N_A A z_+z_-e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r_0}UCoul​=−4πε0​r0​NA​Az+​z−​e2​

A short-range repulsion prevents collapse. In the Born–Landé model, the lattice energy per mole is

U=−NAAz+z−e24πε0r0(1−1n)U=-\frac{N_A A z_+z_-e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r_0}\left(1-\frac1n\right)U=−4πε0​r0​NA​Az+​z−​e2​(1−n1​)

nnn is the Born repulsion exponent and r0r_0r0​ the nearest unlike-ion distance.

  • Higher ionic charges strongly increase lattice-energy magnitude.
  • Smaller nearest-neighbour distance generally strengthens attraction.
  • The Madelung constant depends on structure, so coordination topology matters.
  • Lattice energy contributes to melting point, hardness, defect formation and phase stability, but hydration and entropy also control solubility.
Born–Haber versus Born–Landé

A Born–Haber cycle obtains lattice enthalpy from thermochemical data. Born–Landé estimates it from an electrostatic structural model.

4
Worked example

Charge effect

Compare the electrostatic factor z+z−/r0z_+z_-/r_0z+​z−​/r0​ for NaCl and MgO if their nearest-neighbour distances were equal.

  1. NaCl has ∣z+z−∣=1|z_+z_-|=1∣z+​z−​∣=1.
  2. MgO has ∣z+z−∣=4|z_+z_-|=4∣z+​z−​∣=4.
The Coulomb factor for MgO would be four times as large in magnitude.

7.1 A method for analysing any structure

For every named crystal structure, answer the same questions in order: Which species forms the host lattice? Which holes are occupied? What fraction of those holes is occupied? What is the formula? What are the coordination numbers? How many formula units occur in the conventional cell? What nearest-neighbour geometry connects ionic radii to cell dimensions?

  • Step 1: identify the Bravais lattice and basis, not just the visual positions.
  • Step 2: count each species using boundary fractions.
  • Step 3: determine coordination by actual nearest neighbours.
  • Step 4: derive the nearest-neighbour distance from fractional coordinates.
  • Step 5: check that the counted composition matches charge neutrality.
Structure type versus chemical identity

Many compounds adopt the same structure type. ‘NaCl type’ describes topology and coordination, not the requirement that Na and Cl be present.

7.2 Rock-salt or NaCl structure

Cl−^-− ions may be taken as an FCC array, with Na+^++ ions occupying all octahedral holes. The reverse description is equally valid because both ions form interpenetrating FCC sublattices.

7.3 CsCl structure

One ion occupies the corners of a primitive cubic cell and the other occupies the cubic hole at the body centre. The two chemical sites form a basis on a primitive cubic Bravais lattice.

FeatureCsCl type
Bravais descriptionPrimitive cubic with a two-ion basis
FormulaMX
Coordination8:8
Formula units per cellZ=1Z=1Z=1
Nearest M–X distance3a/2\sqrt3a/23​a/2

Why it is not BCC

A BCC Bravais lattice requires corner and body-centre lattice points to be equivalent. In CsCl they carry different ions, so the Bravais lattice is primitive cubic.

7.4 Zinc blende and wurtzite

Both ZnS polymorphs have tetrahedral 4:4 coordination and half of the tetrahedral holes occupied. They differ in anion stacking: zinc blende uses CCP (ABC), while wurtzite uses HCP (AB).

In zinc blende, the occupied tetrahedral sites may be represented by coordinates such as (1/4,1/4,1/4)(1/4,1/4,1/4)(1/4,1/4,1/4) relative to the FCC anion cell. Only four of the eight tetrahedral holes are occupied.

Worked example

Hole fraction

Anions form CCP and the compound has formula MX with cations only in tetrahedral holes. What fraction of tetrahedral holes is occupied?

  1. For NNN anions, there are 2N2N2N tetrahedral holes.
  2. Formula MX requires NNN cations.
  3. Occupied fraction =N/(2N)=1/2=N/(2N)=1/2=N/(2N)=1/2.
One-half of the tetrahedral holes is occupied.

Worked example

Coordination accounting

In CaF2_22​, how many nearest Ca2+^{2+}2+ neighbours surround each F−^-−, and how many F−^-− surround each Ca2+^{2+}2+?

  1. Fluoride occupies a tetrahedral site in the Ca FCC array, so it has 4 Ca neighbours.

7.6 NiAs and rutile structures

In NiAs, As atoms form an HCP array and Ni atoms occupy all octahedral holes. Each Ni is octahedrally surrounded by six As, while each As is surrounded by six Ni in a trigonal-prismatic arrangement.

StructurePacking/site modelCoordinationFormula
NiAsHCP As; all octahedral holes filled by NiNi 6 (octahedral), As 6 (trigonal prismatic)MX
Rutile TiO2_22​Distorted chains of edge-sharing TiO6_66​ octahedraTi 6, O 3MO2_22​

Rutile is tetragonal. Its TiO6_66​ octahedra are distorted and share edges along one direction and corners between chains. The structure cannot be understood completely as a simple ideal close-packed-hole occupancy.

Same CN does not mean same polyhedron

Both ions in NiAs have coordination number 6, but Ni sees an octahedron whereas As sees a trigonal prism.

7.7 Perovskite structure

In the ideal cubic perovskite ABO3_33​, A occupies cube corners, B the body centre, and O the six face centres. Counting gives one A, one B and three O per cell. B is octahedrally coordinated by oxygen; A occupies a 12-coordinate cuboctahedral cavity.

A-site coordination12
ConnectivityCorner-sharing BO6_66​ octahedra

t=rA+rO2(rB+rO)t=\frac{r_A+r_O}{\sqrt2(r_B+r_O)}t=2​(rB​+rO​)rA​+rO​​

Values below unity often produce tilting of BO6_66​ octahedra; off-centre displacement can produce ferroelectricity, as in BaTiO3_33​. The tolerance factor is empirical and uses coordination-dependent radii.

Count the particles in the ideal cubic ABO3_33​ cell.

  1. A at 8 corners: 8(1/8)=18(1/8)=18(1/8)=1.

7.8 Spinel and inverse spinel

In a spinel AB2_22​O4_44​, oxide ions form an approximately CCP array. Per 32 O2−^{2-}2− conventional spinel cell there are 64 tetrahedral and 32 octahedral holes; only 8 tetrahedral and 16 octahedral sites are occupied by cations.

TypeTetrahedral sitesOctahedral sitesExample
Normal spinelA cationsB cationsMgAl2_22​O4_44​
Inverse spinelHalf of B cationsA plus remaining half of BFe3_33​O4_44​ represented as Fe3+^{3+}3+[Fe2+^{2+}2+Fe3+^{3+}3+]O4_44​

Square brackets are often used for octahedral-site cations. Site preference depends on crystal-field stabilisation, ionic size, charge and synthesis conditions.

Occupancy fractions

Relative to all holes in the oxygen CCP array, a spinel occupies 1/81/81/8 of tetrahedral holes and 1/21/21/2 of octahedral holes.

7.9 Corundum, diamond and graphite

StructureEssential descriptionCoordination
Corundum, Al2_22​O3_33​O approximately HCP; Al occupies 2/32/32/3 of octahedral holesAl 6; O 4
DiamondFCC lattice with (0,0,0)(0,0,0)(0,0,0) and (1/4,1/4,1/4)(1/4,1/4,1/4)(1/4,1/4,1/4) basis; 3D sp3sp^3sp3 networkC 4
GraphiteHexagonal sheets of fused sp2sp^2sp2 carbon rings; weak interlayer forcesC 3 within a layer

Graphite's strong in-plane covalent bonds and weak interlayer interactions explain its anisotropic conductivity, easy cleavage and lubricating behaviour. Diamond's three-dimensional network explains hardness and high thermal conductivity.

Coordination versus bond count

In graphite, each carbon has three nearest covalent neighbours, while the delocalised π\piπ system extends over the layer. Coordination number 3 does not imply three localised single bonds only.

7.11 Wigner–Seitz cell and truncated-octahedron geometry

A Wigner–Seitz cell is the region closer to one lattice point than to any other. It is constructed by drawing perpendicular bisector planes to vectors joining a chosen lattice point to its neighbours. For the BCC lattice, the Wigner–Seitz cell is a truncated octahedron.

Truncated-octahedron featureValue
Total faces14
Regular hexagonal faces8
Square faces6
Edges36
Vertices24
Why it appears in crystallography

The Wigner–Seitz cell is always primitive: it contains one lattice point. Its shape need not resemble the conventional cubic cell.

PART 5

Imperfections in solids

Real crystals are never perfect. Missing, displaced and foreign atoms explain density changes, colour, conductivity and the strength of metals.

An ideal crystal has every particle on its lattice site. Real crystals above absolute zero contain defects: faults in the regular arrangement. They are classified by their size. Point defects involve single sites; line defects (dislocations) run through the crystal along a line; plane and volume defects include grain boundaries, stacking faults, voids and cracks.

Point defects divide further. Stoichiometric defects leave the ratio of cations to anions exactly as in the formula (Schottky, Frenkel). Non-stoichiometric defects change the ratio (metal excess, metal deficiency). Impurity defects bring in foreign ions.

PerfectSchottkyFrenkelF-centreExtra cationsMetal deficiencyImpurity
Schottky defect: a missing cation–anion pair
  • Equal numbers of cations and anions are missing, so the crystal stays neutral and keeps its formula.
  • The ions end up on the surface, so the volume grows while the mass does not: density falls.
  • Favoured when cations and anions are similar in size and coordination is high.
  • More pairs form as temperature rises.
Class
Stoichiometric
Density
decreases
Found in
NaCl, KCl, CsCl, AgBr
Charge
balanced
PropertySchottkyFrenkel
What happensA cation and an anion leave the latticeAn ion moves into an interstitial site
VacanciesTwo (one of each ion)One, plus one interstitial
DensityDecreasesUnchanged
Favoured bySimilar ion sizes, high coordinationLarge size difference, low coordination
ExamplesNaCl, KCl, CsCl, AgBrZnS, AgCl, AgBr, AgI

How many defects form?

Defects cost energy to make but increase disorder (entropy), so a crystal at equilibrium always contains some. The number of Schottky pairs follows a Boltzmann factor, rising steeply with temperature:

nsN≈exp⁡ ⁣(−ΔHs2kT)\dfrac{n_s}{N} \approx \exp\!\left(-\dfrac{\Delta H_s}{2kT}\right)Nns​​≈exp(−2kTΔHs​​)
4.0 × 10-9
fraction of sites vacant (pairs per ion pair)
About 2.4e+15 pairs per mole of crystal
Derivation 5.1

Why the factor is exp(−ΔH / 2kT)

Given
A crystal of NNN cation sites and NNN anion sites. Forming one Schottky pair (a cation vacancy and an anion vacancy) costs enthalpy ΔH\Delta HΔH.
To find
The equilibrium number nnn of Schottky pairs at temperature TTT.
  1. 1
    Creating nnn Schottky pairs in a crystal of NNN ion pairs costs energy n ΔHn\,\Delta HnΔH but raises the number of arrangements WWW in which the vacancies could sit.
  2. 2
    Choose which nnn of NNN cation sites and which nnn of NNN anion sites are empty:
    W=(Nn)2⇒S=kln⁡W≈2k [ Nln⁡N−nln⁡n−(N−n)ln⁡(N−n) ]W = \binom{N}{n}^2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad S = k\ln W \approx 2k\,[\,N\ln N - n\ln n - (N-n)\ln(N-n)\,]W=(nN​)2⇒S=klnW≈2k[NlnN−nlnn−(N−n)ln(N−n)](1)
  3. 3
    Minimise the free energy G=n ΔH−TSG = n\,\Delta H - TSG=nΔH−TS with respect to nnn (set dG/dn=0dG/dn = 0dG/dn=0) and use n≪Nn \ll Nn≪N:
    ΔH=2kTln⁡N−nn  ≈  2kTln⁡Nn\Delta H = 2kT\ln\frac{N-n}{n} \;\approx\; 2kT\ln\frac{N}{n}ΔH=2kTlnnN−n​≈2kTlnnN​(2)
Hence
n≈Nexp⁡ ⁣(−ΔH2kT)n \approx N\exp\!\left(-\dfrac{\Delta H}{2kT}\right)n≈Nexp(−2kTΔH​)∎

Derivation 5.2

Density of a crystal with Schottky or Frenkel defects

Given
A crystal of NNN formula units in which nnn Schottky pairs have formed (each pair removes one cation and one anion from the crystal), with the same cell volume.
To find
How the density changes compared with the perfect crystal.
  1. 1
    Density is mass divided by volume. A Schottky pair takes two ions out of the crystal, so the mass falls while the volume stays the same:
    ρ=mV  ⟶  ρ′=m−n mpairV\rho = \frac{m}{V} \;\longrightarrow\; \rho' = \frac{m - n\,m_{\text{pair}}}{V}ρ=Vm​⟶ρ′=Vm−nmpair​​(1)
  2. 2
    The mass of NNN formula units is N mpairN\,m_{\text{pair}}Nmpair​, so:
    ρ′=ρ N−nN<ρ\rho' = \rho\,\frac{N-n}{N} < \rhoρ′=ρNN−n​<ρ(2)
  3. 3
    In a Frenkel defect the ion only moves from a lattice site to an interstitial site. No ion leaves the crystal and the volume is unchanged, so ρ′=ρ\rho' = \rhoρ′=ρ.
Hence
Schottky: density falls;Frenkel: density unchanged\text{Schottky: density falls};\qquad \text{Frenkel: density unchanged}Schottky: density falls;Frenkel: density unchanged∎

Metal-excess defects (F-centres) and metal-deficiency defects are also compositional: the density of Fe0.95_{0.95}0.95​O is lower than that of ideal FeO because some sites are vacant.

A crystal with NNN lattice sites for the displaced ion and NiN_iNi​ interstitial sites available to it. Moving one ion from a lattice site to an interstitial site costs enthalpy DeltaH\\Delta HDeltaH.
To find
The equilibrium number nnn of Frenkel defects at temperature TTT.

    Choose which nnn of the NNN lattice sites are vacated, and which nnn of the NiN_iNi​ interstitial sites are filled:
    W=(Nn)(Nin)W = \binom{N}{n}\binom{N_i}{n}W=(nN​)(nNi​​)(1)
  2. 2
    Boltzmann's entropy with Stirling's approximation ln⁡x!≈xln⁡x−x\ln x! \approx x\ln x - xlnx!≈xlnx−x gives:

Hence
n=NNi  exp⁡ ⁣(−ΔH2kT)n = \sqrt{N N_i}\;\exp\!\left(-\dfrac{\Delta H}{2kT}\right)n=NNi​​exp(−2kTΔH​)∎

Compare derivation 5.1: for Schottky defects the two sets of sites are equal, Ni→NN_i \to NNi​→N, and the same factor e−ΔH/2kTe^{-\Delta H/2kT}e−ΔH/2kT appears. The factor of two in the exponent comes from creating the vacancy and its partner together.

Line defects: dislocations

A dislocation is a line along which the crystal is out of step with itself. In the edge form an extra half-plane of atoms is inserted; in the screw form the planes spiral around the line like a ramp. The Burgers vector b measures the size and direction of the lattice slip. Move the defect with shear stress and watch the crystal deform.

▶ Apply shear stressReset
Edge dislocation. An extra half-plane of atoms (white mark) is squeezed in from above. Atoms above the line are compressed (rose), below it stretched (blue). Under shear the defect glides one row at a time, so only a few bonds break at once.
Line defect
dislocation
Burgers vector b
one lattice spacing
Edge type
line ⟂ b
Screw type
line ∥ b

Slipping a whole plane at once would need a stress close to G/10 (G is the shear modulus). Moving a dislocation needs about a thousandth of that. This is why real metals are far softer than their bond strengths suggest, and why bending a paper clip makes it harder: dislocations tangle and block each other.

Plane and volume defects
Grain boundaries separate crystals of different orientation (every ordinary metal is a patchwork of grains). Stacking faults are a missing or extra layer in an ABC… sequence. Voids, cracks and inclusions are three-dimensional gaps or foreign particles. All of them act as barriers to dislocations, which is why small-grained metals are stronger.

Defects and electrical conduction

Defects are what allow an ionic solid to conduct. A perfect NaCl crystal has no free charge carrier, but each vacancy gives a neighbouring ion somewhere to go. Under an electric field, ions hop into vacancies one after another.

▶ Apply the fieldReset
A cation vacancy (dashed) sits in the crystal. With no field, ions hop in random directions.

More vacancies (higher temperature, or doping with SrCl₂) means more hops available, so conductivity rises.

JEE traps
  • Schottky lowers the density; Frenkel does not. Both are stoichiometric.
  • AgBr shows both Schottky and Frenkel defects; NaCl shows Schottky only; ZnS Frenkel only.
  • F-centre = anion vacancy + trapped electron; the colour comes from the electron. KCl is violet, NaCl yellow, LiCl pink.
  • In metal deficiency the oxidation state rises (Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺) to compensate for the missing cation.
  • Doping with a higher-valent ion (Sr²⁺ in NaCl) creates one vacancy per dopant ion, independent of temperature.
