8.1 Perfect crystals and real crystals

A perfect crystal is an ideal reference in which every lattice site has its prescribed occupant and the periodic arrangement extends without interruption. At any temperature above absolute zero, real crystals contain thermodynamically generated point defects. Additional defects arise during growth, deformation, irradiation and doping.

DimensionalityDefect classExamples
0DPoint defectVacancy, interstitial, substitutional impurity
1DLine defectEdge and screw dislocations
2DPlanar defectGrain boundary, stacking fault, twin boundary
3DVolume defectPore, inclusion, precipitate

The elementary chemistry chapter concentrates on point defects because they directly affect stoichiometry, density, colour and electrical behaviour.

8.2 Stoichiometric intrinsic defects

A stoichiometric defect preserves the overall cation:anion ratio of the ideal compound.

DefectMicroscopic eventDensity effectTypical conditions/examples
Vacancy defect in an elemental solidAn atom is absent from a normal siteDecreasesHigh temperature
Interstitial defect in an elemental solidAn extra atom occupies an interstitial siteIncreasesSmall atoms/open structures
Schottky defectEqual stoichiometric numbers of cations and anions are missingDecreasesHigh coordination, similar ion sizes: NaCl, KCl, CsCl
Frenkel defectA smaller ion leaves its site and occupies an interstitial positionApproximately unchangedLarge size difference, lower CN: AgCl, AgBr, ZnS
ρdefective<ρidealfor Schottky disorder\rho_{defective}<\rho_{ideal}\quad\text{for Schottky disorder}ρdefective​<ρideal​for Schottky disorder
ρdefective≈ρidealfor Frenkel disorder\rho_{defective}\approx\rho_{ideal}\quad\text{for Frenkel disorder}ρdefective​≈ρideal​for Frenkel disorder
AgBr can show both

Silver bromide can exhibit both Schottky and Frenkel disorder. Lists of ‘typical examples’ are trends, not exclusive laws.

8.3 Thermodynamics of defect formation

Creating a defect costs enthalpy but increases configurational entropy. The equilibrium concentration therefore increases with temperature.

n≈Nexp⁡(−ΔHfkT)n\approx N\exp\left(-\frac{\Delta H_f}{kT}\right)n≈Nexp(−kTΔHf​​)

Schematic dependence for independent point defects; exact prefactors and exponents depend on the defect reaction.

Derivation · Schottky-pair scaling
KS∝(nN)2K_S\propto\left(\frac{n}{N}\right)^2KS​∝(Nn​)2

A neutral pair contains one cation vacancy and one anion vacancy.

KS=exp⁡(−ΔGSkT)K_S=\exp\left(-\frac{\Delta G_S}{kT}\right)KS​=exp(−kTΔGS​​)

Equilibrium follows the free energy of pair formation.

Result
nN∝exp⁡(−ΔGS2kT)\frac{n}{N}\propto\exp\left(-\frac{\Delta G_S}{2kT}\right)Nn​∝exp(−2kTΔGS​​)

JEE questions usually test the qualitative trend: defect concentration rises exponentially with temperature and falls as formation energy increases.

8.4 Impurity defects and charge compensation

A substitutional impurity of different charge requires compensation to preserve macroscopic electroneutrality. Compensation can occur through vacancies, interstitials or changes in oxidation state.

1
Worked example

SrCl$_2$ doped NaCl

A crystal contains 10−310^{-3}10−3 mol SrCl2_22​ substitutionally dissolved in 1 mol NaCl. Neglect other defects. How many Na+^++ vacancies are created?

  1. Each Sr2+^{2+}2+ occupies one Na+^++ site but supplies one extra positive charge relative to Na+^++.
  2. One Na+^++ vacancy, carrying one effective negative charge, compensates each Sr2+^{2+}2+ substitution.
  3. Therefore moles of Na vacancies equal moles of SrCl2_22​.
10−310^{-3}10−3 mol of Na+^++ vacancies are created.
SrCl2 in NaCl:[VNa]=[SrNa∙]\mathrm{SrCl_2\ in\ NaCl}:\quad [V_{Na}]=[Sr_{Na}^{\bullet}]SrCl2​ in NaCl:[VNa​]=[SrNa∙​]

Effective-charge notation is shown schematically.

Vacancy count, not missing pairs

One divalent cation replacing a monovalent cation creates one monovalent-cation vacancy per dopant, not one anion vacancy.

8.5 Metal-excess defects

A metal-excess solid contains effectively more metal than required by the ideal stoichiometric ratio, usually because negative charge is stored as electrons.

MechanismDescriptionExample/effect
Anion vacancy with trapped electronAn anion leaves; an electron occupies the vacancy to maintain neutrality. The electron-containing vacancy is an F-centre.NaCl heated in Na vapour; yellow colour
Interstitial cation plus electronExtra metal ions enter interstitial sites and electrons occupy nearby interstitial regions or conduction states.ZnO on heating loses O2_22​ and becomes yellow, n-type
OO→12O2(g)+VO∙∙+2e−\mathrm{O_O\rightarrow\tfrac12O_2(g)+V_O^{\bullet\bullet}+2e^-}OO​→21​O2​(g)+VO∙∙​+2e−

F-centres absorb visible light because the trapped electron has quantised states in the vacancy potential. The absorbed wavelength and observed colour depend on the host lattice.

2
Worked example

Stoichiometry of oxygen-deficient ZnO

Write the qualitative formula of zinc oxide after slight oxygen loss.

  1. Oxygen vacancies reduce the oxygen content below one per zinc.
  2. Electrons left behind preserve charge balance and produce n-type conductivity.
The composition is written ZnO1−x\mathrm{ZnO_{1-x}}ZnO1−x​ with x>0x>0x>0.

8.6 Metal-deficiency defects

Metal deficiency commonly occurs when a metal can adopt more than one oxidation state. Some lower-valent cation sites are vacant, while other cations oxidise to maintain electroneutrality.

In wüstite, often written Fe1−x_{1-x}1−x​O, some Fe2+^{2+}2+ sites are vacant and a corresponding fraction of Fe2+^{2+}2+ ions becomes Fe3+^{3+}3+.

3
Worked example

Fe$_{0.95}$O oxidation-state fraction

Assume oxide is O2−^{2-}2−. In Fe0.95_{0.95}0.95​O, let yyy mol of iron per formula be Fe3+^{3+}3+ and the rest Fe2+^{2+}2+. Find yyy.

  1. Charge balance: 3y+2(0.95−y)=23y+2(0.95-y)=23y+2(0.95−y)=2.
  2. 3y+1.90−2y=23y+1.90-2y=23y+1.90−2y=2.
  3. y=0.10y=0.10y=0.10.
Per Fe0.95_{0.95}0.95​O, 0.10 Fe is Fe3+^{3+}3+ and 0.85 Fe is Fe2+^{2+}2+; about 10.53% of occupied Fe sites are Fe3+^{3+}3+.

8.7 Density changes caused by defects

The theoretical density formula can be modified by replacing the ideal cell mass with the actual mass after defects. Cell-volume change is often neglected in elementary problems unless stated.

ρ′=mideal−mmissing+maddedVcell\rho'=\frac{m_{ideal}-m_{missing}+m_{added}}{V_{cell}}ρ′=Vcell​mideal​−mmissing​+madded​​
4
Worked example

Schottky fraction from density

A crystal has ideal density ρ0\rho_0ρ0​ and measured density 0.99ρ00.99\rho_00.99ρ0​. Assume the cell volume is unchanged and only whole formula units are missing through Schottky defects. Estimate the fraction of formula units missing.

  1. Density is proportional to mass per cell when volume is unchanged.
  2. ρ/ρ0=0.99\rho/\rho_0=0.99ρ/ρ0​=0.99 means 99% of ideal mass remains.
  3. Missing fraction is 1%.
Approximately 1% of formula units are absent.

8.8 Extended defects and mechanical behaviour

Dislocations allow plastic deformation at stresses far below those required to shear an entire perfect plane simultaneously. Grain boundaries interrupt periodicity and can impede dislocation motion, which is why reducing grain size often strengthens metals.

DefectStructural ideaImportant consequence
Edge dislocationExtra half-plane of atomsPlastic slip
Screw dislocationHelical mismatch around a linePlastic slip and crystal growth
Stacking faultIncorrect local layer sequenceChanges close-packed polytype/local energy
Grain boundaryInterface between orientationsDiffusion path; can strengthen or embrittle
Scope

Detailed dislocation theory is beyond the standard JEE syllabus, but recognising the link between defects and real mechanical properties prevents the false idea that defects are merely imperfections with no function.

PART 6

Electrical properties of solids

Why does copper conduct, diamond insulate and silicon do both under the right conditions? The answer is bands: what happens to atomic energy levels when N atoms come together.

From atoms to bands

In molecular orbital theory two atomic orbitals combine to make two molecular orbitals. N atoms make N molecular orbitals, spaced so closely that they form a nearly continuous band. Each band is separated from the next by a forbidden gap. Which bands are filled decides whether the solid conducts.

▶ Bring the atoms togetherPull apart
1 e⁻ per atom (like Na)2 e⁻ per atom (like Mg)3 e⁻ per atom
Isolated atoms
Each atom has its own sharp levels. The ten atoms' levels coincide.

This is a tight-binding model: for a chain of N atoms the N levels of each orbital are Ek=ε−2βcos⁡ ⁣(kπN+1)E_k = \varepsilon - 2\beta\cos\!\left(\tfrac{k\pi}{N+1}\right)Ek​=ε−2βcos(N+1kπ​), k = 1 … N. The hopping energy β grows as the atoms approach, so the levels spread into a band of width 4β. Each level holds two electrons.

Conductor

A partly filled band, or filled and empty bands that overlap. Electrons just below the Fermi level can move into empty states with almost no energy.

Cu, Ag, Na, Mg

Semiconductor

A filled valence band, an empty conduction band, and a small gap (about 0.5–3 eV). Heat, light or doping supplies carriers.

Si 1.1 eV, Ge 0.67 eV

Insulator

A filled valence band and a large gap (greater than about 3 eV). No carriers at ordinary temperatures.

Diamond 5.5 eV, SiO₂

Who is excited? The Fermi–Dirac distribution

Electrons obey the Pauli principle, so the chance that a state at energy EEE is occupied is given by the Fermi–Dirac distribution. It is a Boltzmann factor corrected for the fact that no orbital holds more than two electrons. EFE_FEF​, the Fermi energy, is the energy at which the occupation probability is exactly ½. At T=0T = 0T=0 it is a sharp step: everything below EFE_FEF​ is full and everything above is empty. As the temperature rises the step blurs and an exponential tail reaches above EFE_FEF​.

At the bottom of the conduction band, E−EF=Eg/2=0.55E - E_F = E_g/2 = 0.55E−EF​=Eg​/2=0.55 eV, the occupation probability is 2.4×10−52.4\times10^{-5}2.4×10−5. That tiny tail is the whole supply of conduction electrons. At T=0T = 0T=0 the curve is a step and the band stays empty.
f(E)=1e(E−EF)/kT+1f(E) = \dfrac{1}{e^{(E-E_F)/kT} + 1}f(E)=e(E−EF​)/kT+11​
Fermi–Dirac distribution. At E = E_F the probability is exactly ½ at any T.
kT

The Fermi level is the top filled level at T=0T = 0T=0. The Fermi energy is the energy where f=12f = \tfrac12f=21​ at any temperature. They coincide as T→0T \to 0T→0. For energies well above EFE_FEF​ the 1 in the denominator is negligible and f≈e−(E−EF)/kTf \approx e^{-(E-E_F)/kT}f≈e−(E−EF​)/kT, a pure Boltzmann tail. In an intrinsic semiconductor EFE_FEF​ sits mid-gap, so the conduction band edge is Eg/2E_g/2Eg​/2 above it: this is the origin of the factor e−Eg/2kTe^{-E_g/2kT}e−Eg​/2kT in the next section.

A metal's conductivity falls as it heats because lattice vibrations scatter the electrons. A semiconductor's conductivity rises as it heats because more electrons are promoted across the gap.

Why conductivity of a semiconductor grows as exp(−Eg / 2kT)

Given
An intrinsic semiconductor with band gap EgE_gEg​ at temperature TTT.
To find

  1. 1
    In a pure semiconductor the Fermi level sits in the middle of the gap, so the conduction band edge is Eg/2E_g/2Eg​/2 above it.
  2. 2
    The probability that a state at energy EEE above the Fermi level is occupied falls as a Boltzmann factor e−E/kTe^{-E/kT}e−E/kT. For states at the bottom of the conduction band:

Doping: extrinsic semiconductors

Pure silicon conducts poorly. Adding a trace of another element, doping, changes that dramatically. A group 15 atom brings one electron more than silicon needs (n-type); a group 13 atom brings one less, creating a hole (p-type). Both are extrinsic semiconductors.

Intrinsicn-type (donor)p-type (acceptor)
n-type. Replace a few silicon atoms (4 valence electrons) by phosphorus or arsenic (5). The extra electron sits just below the conduction band and is freed by a little heat. Majority carriers: electrons (negative).
Dopant group
15 (P, As, Sb)
Majority carrier
electrons
Whole crystal
electrically neutral
High temperature
intrinsic carriers take over

Doping with one atom in about 10⁶ raises the conductivity of silicon by a factor of order 10⁶. Compound semiconductors mix group 13 with 15 (GaAs, InP) or group 12 with 16 (ZnS, CdS, CdSe).

The p–n junction

Join a p-type and an n-type crystal and you have a diode. Electrons from the n side and holes from the p side cross the boundary and annihilate, leaving a charged, carrier-free depletion layer that acts as a barrier. A voltage applied across it opens or closes the gate.

Reverse biasNo biasForward bias
No bias. Holes from the p side and electrons from the n side diffuse across and annihilate near the junction. They leave behind fixed ions: negative acceptors on the p side, positive donors on the n side. These build an electric field that stops further diffusion. The carrier-free zone is the depletion layer.
Depletion layer
equilibrium width
Current
≈ 0 (leakage)
Acts as
one-way valve
Uses
rectifier, LED, solar cell

The curve shows why a p-n junction is a rectifier: it conducts in one direction only. In an LED, electrons and holes recombine under forward bias and release the gap energy as light; a solar cell runs the process backwards.

Superconductors

Some materials lose all electrical resistance below a critical temperature, written TcT_cTc​. Dutch physicist Kamerlingh Onnes found it in mercury at 4.2 K in 1911. A superconductor also expels magnetic fields from its interior, the Meissner effect.

Mercury (4.2 K)Lead (7.2 K)Nb₃Sn (18 K)YBa₂Cu₃O₇ (92 K)
Above the critical temperature the material is an ordinary metal. Its resistance decreases as it cools but never vanishes, and the magnetic field passes straight through.
Zero resistance
below Tc
Meissner effect
field expelled
Susceptibility
χ = −1
Liquid nitrogen (77 K)
too warm

Below Tc electrons pair up (Cooper pairs) and move through the lattice without scattering. Superconductors work in MRI magnets, maglev trains and particle accelerators. Ceramic oxides such as YBa₂Cu₃O₇ (92 K) work above the boiling point of liquid nitrogen.

Critical field and the two types of superconductor

A strong enough magnetic field destroys superconductivity. For a Type I superconductor (the pure metals such as lead, mercury and tin) there is a single critical field HcH_cHc​, and superconductivity is lost abruptly when it is exceeded. Below HcH_cHc​ the material is a perfect diamagnet. The critical field falls with temperature and vanishes at TcT_cTc​. Explore the boundary.

Normal. At 6.0 K the critical field is only 19.4 kA/m. The applied 30 kA/m exceeds it and destroys the superconducting state abruptly.
Hc(T)=Hc(0)(1−T2Tc2)H_c(T) = H_c(0)\left(1 - \dfrac{T^2}{T_c^2}\right)Hc​(T)=Hc​(0)(1−Tc2​T2​)
Empirical, valid for T ≤ Tc. Defaults are lead.
Type I and Type II
Type I: one critical field, abrupt loss of superconductivity, complete Meissner effect below it. Pure metals. Type II: two critical fields. Between them the field partly penetrates in threads (vortices) and diamagnetism is lost gradually. Alloys, intermetallics such as Nb₃Sn and all the high-temperature ceramics such as YBa₂Cu₃O₇. Type II materials tolerate far stronger fields, which is why they wind the magnets of MRI scanners.
Cooper pairs
One electron slightly distorts the lattice, pulling the positive nuclei toward it. That patch of extra positive charge attracts a second electron. The two electrons form a Cooper pair, bound by a virtual attraction through the lattice. Thermal motion disrupts the distortion, so pairing survives only at very low temperature. A pair is much less likely to be scattered than a single electron, so it carries current without resistance.

JEE traps
  • Metal: σ decreases on heating. Semiconductor: σ increases on heating.
  • An n-type or p-type crystal is electrically neutral: the donor atom's extra electron is balanced by an extra proton in the dopant's nucleus.
  • A hole is the absence of an electron in the valence band, not a particle. It behaves as a positive carrier.
  • n-type: group 15 dopant (P, As); p-type: group 13 dopant (B, Al, Ga). Compound semiconductors: 13–15 (GaAs) and 12–16 (ZnS, CdS).
  • In a forward-biased diode the depletion layer narrows; in reverse it widens.

9.1 From atomic orbitals to energy bands

When a very large number of atoms forms a solid, each atomic orbital splits into an enormous number of closely spaced crystal orbitals. These levels merge into allowed energy bands separated by forbidden energy gaps.

TermMeaning
Valence bandHighest band occupied at absolute zero in an ordinary semiconductor or insulator
Conduction bandHigher band whose mobile carriers can transport charge
Band gap EgE_gEg​Forbidden energy interval between valence- and conduction-band edges
Fermi level EFE_FEF​Chemical potential for electrons; at 0 K it separates occupied and unoccupied states

Electrical conduction requires both mobile charge carriers and nearby unoccupied states into which they can move under an electric field.

9.2 Conductors, semiconductors and insulators

ClassBand pictureTemperature dependence of conductivity
MetalPartially filled band or overlapping bandsUsually decreases as temperature rises because lattice scattering increases
SemiconductorSmall band gap, typically of order electron-volts or lessIncreases strongly with temperature as carriers are generated
InsulatorLarge band gapRemains very low under ordinary conditions
σ=nqμ\sigma=nq\muσ=nqμ

For one carrier type: number density nnn, charge magnitude qqq, mobility μ\muμ.

In a metal, carrier density is already large and temperature mainly changes mobility. In a semiconductor, thermal excitation changes carrier density dramatically, often dominating the mobility decrease.

1
Worked example

Temperature trend

Why does the resistance of a pure semiconductor usually fall on heating while that of a metal rises?

  1. Heating a semiconductor promotes many more electrons across the band gap, increasing carrier density.
  2. Heating a metal mainly increases phonon scattering, reducing mobility.
  3. The dominant effects therefore have opposite signs.
Semiconductor conductivity rises; metallic conductivity usually falls with temperature.

9.3 Intrinsic semiconductors

An intrinsic semiconductor is chemically pure in the ideal model. Thermal excitation creates an electron in the conduction band and a corresponding hole in the valence band.

n=p=nin=p=n_in=p=ni​
σi=qni(μe+μh)\sigma_i=q n_i(\mu_e+\mu_h)σi​=qni​(μe​+μh​)
ni∝T3/2exp⁡(−Eg2kT)n_i\propto T^{3/2}\exp\left(-\frac{E_g}{2kT}\right)ni​∝T3/2exp(−2kTEg​​)

A hole is not a separate positive particle in vacuum; it is a convenient description of the collective motion of missing valence electrons. Under an electric field, electron and hole currents add to the conventional current.

Fermi level

For a symmetric ideal intrinsic semiconductor, EFE_FEF​ lies near the middle of the gap. Different electron and hole effective masses shift it slightly.

9.4 Extrinsic semiconductors

Controlled substitutional doping introduces shallow energy levels and greatly increases carrier density without destroying the crystal lattice.

TypeDopant in Si/GeMajority carrierMinority carrierFermi-level shift
n-typeGroup 15 donor: P, As, SbElectronsHolesToward conduction band
p-typeGroup 13 acceptor: B, Al, GaHolesElectronsToward valence band

In n-type material, donor atoms contribute electrons but become fixed positively charged donor ions after ionisation. The crystal remains electrically neutral overall. Similarly, ionised acceptors are fixed negative centres in p-type material.

n-type is not negatively charged

The labels n and p identify the majority mobile carrier. They do not mean the bulk solid carries net negative or positive charge.

2
Worked example

Dopant choice

Which dopant converts silicon into p-type material: phosphorus or boron? Explain.

  1. Silicon has four valence electrons.
  2. Boron has three and leaves one unsatisfied bond that acts as an acceptor level.
  3. Thermal excitation fills the acceptor and leaves a mobile hole.
Boron produces p-type silicon.

9.5 The p–n junction

When p-type and n-type regions meet, majority carriers diffuse across the interface and recombine. Fixed ionised donors and acceptors remain, creating a depletion region and an internal electric field that opposes further diffusion.

BiasEffect on barrier/depletion widthCurrent
Forward biasReduces barrier and narrows depletion regionLarge majority-carrier current
Reverse biasRaises effective barrier and widens depletion regionSmall minority-carrier current until breakdown

Rectification follows because the junction conducts much more readily in forward bias than in reverse bias. Light can generate electron–hole pairs, enabling photodiodes and solar cells.

3
Worked example

Forward-bias identification

For a silicon diode, which terminal should be connected to the p side for forward bias?

  1. Forward bias must lower the junction barrier.
  2. Connect the p region to the positive terminal and the n region to the negative terminal.
Positive to p and negative to n gives forward bias.

9.6 Ionic and mixed conduction

In ionic solids, charge can be transported by ions moving through vacancies or interstitial pathways. Ionic conductivity therefore depends strongly on defect concentration, migration energy and temperature.

σion∝ndefectexp⁡(−EmkT)\sigma_{ion}\propto n_{defect}\exp\left(-\frac{E_m}{kT}\right)σion​∝ndefect​exp(−kTEm​​)

Fast-ion conductors such as stabilised zirconia, beta-alumina and some fluorite oxides have connected pathways and abundant mobile defects. Some materials conduct both ions and electrons and are called mixed conductors.

Solid ionic conductors exist

The elementary rule ‘ionic solids do not conduct’ means ordinary defect-poor crystals conduct poorly at room temperature. It is not an absolute statement for all solids and temperatures.

9.7 Superconductivity

A superconductor below its critical temperature exhibits zero dc electrical resistance and expels magnetic flux from its interior, the Meissner effect. Perfect conductivity alone does not define superconductivity; magnetic flux expulsion is essential.

QuantityMeaning
Critical temperature TcT_cTc​Highest temperature for the superconducting state at specified field/current
Critical field HcH_cHc​ or Hc1,Hc2H_{c1},H_{c2}Hc1​,Hc2​Magnetic-field limits of the superconducting state
Critical current density JcJ_cJc​Current-density limit before superconductivity is destroyed
Meissner effectExpulsion of magnetic flux on cooling through TcT_cTc​

Type I superconductors show one critical field and complete flux exclusion below it. Type II superconductors have a mixed vortex state between lower and upper critical fields and are more useful in high-field magnets.

BCS and high-$T_c$ materials

Conventional superconductors are described by Cooper pairing mediated by lattice vibrations. Cuprate high-TcT_cTc​ superconductors are more complex; detailed microscopic theory is outside the JEE syllabus.

9.8 Numerical relations and diagnostic plots

4
Worked example

Intrinsic carrier ratio

Two intrinsic semiconductors at the same temperature have gaps 1.0 eV and 1.4 eV. Ignoring prefactors, find the ratio ni,1/ni,2n_{i,1}/n_{i,2}ni,1​/ni,2​ at 300 K, where kT≈0.0259kT\approx0.0259kT≈0.0259 eV.

  1. ni∝exp⁡[−Eg/(2kT)]n_i\propto\exp[-E_g/(2kT)]ni​∝exp[−Eg​/(2kT)].
  2. Ratio =exp⁡[(1.4−1.0)/(2×0.0259)]=\exp[(1.4-1.0)/(2\times0.0259)]=exp[(1.4−1.0)/(2×0.0259)].
  3. Exponent ≈7.72\approx7.72≈7.72, so ratio ≈2.25×103\approx2.25\times10^3≈2.25×103.
The smaller-gap semiconductor has roughly 2.3×1032.3\times10^32.3×103 times the intrinsic carrier density.

A plot of ln⁡σ\ln\sigmalnσ or ln⁡ni\ln n_ilnni​ against 1/T1/T1/T is approximately linear in an activated regime. The slope can be used to estimate an activation energy or half the band gap, depending on the measured quantity and assumptions.

9.9 Fermi–Dirac occupancy

The probability that an available one-electron state of energy EEE is occupied at temperature TTT is given by the Fermi–Dirac distribution.

f(E)=11+exp⁡[(E−EF)/(kT)]f(E)=\frac{1}{1+\exp[(E-E_F)/(kT)]}f(E)=1+exp[(E−EF​)/(kT)]1​
  • At E=EFE=E_FE=EF​, f=1/2f=1/2f=1/2 at every non-zero temperature.
  • At 0 K, states below EFE_FEF​ are occupied and those above are empty.
  • Thermal broadening occurs over an energy scale of order kTkTkT.
Band occupancy is not carrier density by itself

Carrier concentration also depends on the density of available states. The Fermi function supplies the occupation probability.

9.10 Purification and liquid-crystal materials

Semiconductor devices require extremely pure material. In zone refining, a narrow molten zone moves along a solid bar. When an impurity has distribution coefficient k=Csolid/Cliquid<1k=C_{solid}/C_{liquid}<1k=Csolid​/Cliquid​<1, it prefers the melt and is swept toward one end through repeated passes.

Liquid crystals combine fluidity with orientational order. Nematic phases possess average molecular alignment without layered positional order; smectic phases possess layers; cholesteric phases show a helical director. Their optical anisotropy can be controlled by electric fields.

PhaseOrientational orderLayering
NematicYesNo
SmecticYesYes
CholestericLocally nematic with helical twistNo simple equally spaced layers required
LCD principle

A twisted-nematic display uses field-controlled molecular orientation to change the polarisation state and transmitted intensity of light between polarisers.

Part review

1

Bands arise from splitting of atomic levels in a periodic solid.

2

Metals have available nearby states; semiconductors have a small gap; insulators a large gap.

3

Intrinsic semiconductors satisfy n=pn=pn=p.

4

Donors create n-type and acceptors p-type material without net bulk charge.

5

Superconductivity requires zero resistance and the Meissner effect.

PART 7

Magnetic properties

Every electron is a tiny magnet. Whether a solid is attracted, repelled, or can itself become a magnet depends on whether those tiny magnets cancel, point randomly, or line up.

An electron has a magnetic moment from two motions: its spin and its orbital motion around the nucleus. Electrons in the same orbital have opposite spins, so their moments cancel. A substance's magnetic behaviour is therefore set by how many unpaired electrons it has and how the resulting atomic moments interact with each other. The unit of magnetic moment is the Bohr magneton (BM).

How many unpaired electrons?

For transition-metal ions the orbital contribution is largely quenched, so the moment is close to the spin-only value. Fill the five 3d orbitals following Hund's rule and count the unpaired electrons.

4 unpaired electrons: paramagnetic.

Susceptibility, Curie's law and how it is measured

The magnetisation MMM is the average moment per molecule times the number density. It is proportional to the applied field strength HHH: M=χHM = \chi HM=χH, where χ\chiχ is the dimensionless volume susceptibility. The molar susceptibility is χm=χVm\chi_m = \chi V_mχm​=χVm​. A substance with χ>0\chi > 0χ>0 is paramagnetic: it is drawn into the field and the lines of force crowd into it. One with χ<0\chi < 0χ<0 is diamagnetic: it is pushed out and the lines thin out inside it.

With 3 unpaired electrons, S=1.5S = 1.5S=1.5 and the spin-only moment is 3.88 μB3.88\,\mu_B3.88μB​. Double the temperature and χ halves, because thermal motion scrambles the alignment of the spins.
Molar χm
7.93 × 10⁻⁸ m³/mol
Volume χ
1.28 × 10^-3
Spin-only moment
3.88 μB
Curie constant C
23.6 × 10⁻⁶
How susceptibility is measured
In a Gouy balance the sample hangs in a narrow tube between the poles of a magnet. A paramagnetic sample is pulled in and appears heavier when the field is on; a diamagnetic one is pushed out and appears lighter. The balance is calibrated with a sample of known susceptibility. Modern instruments use a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), an extremely sensitive magnetometer built from a superconducting loop.
Orbital paramagnetism (TIP)
Every molecule has a diamagnetic part, from currents induced in its filled orbitals. Spin paramagnetism usually overwhelms it when there are unpaired electrons. A few molecules with no unpaired electrons are paramagnetic anyway, because the induced currents can use empty orbitals lying close above the HOMO. This effect is independent of temperature and is called temperature-independent paramagnetism (TIP).

Five kinds of magnetic behaviour

DiamagneticParamagneticFerromagneticAntiferromagneticFerrimagnetic
Ferromagnetic

Neighbouring moments lock parallel in domains. The solid is strongly attracted and can stay magnetised after the field is removed.

Examples: Fe, Co, Ni, CrO₂

Curie temperature: Fe 1043 K, Ni 627 K

Net moment per site0.99

Domains and hysteresis

In a ferromagnet, moments align in small regions called domains. In an unmagnetised piece the domains point every way and cancel. An applied field makes domains aligned with it grow and flip the others. Take the field away and some stay flipped: the piece has become a magnet.

▶ Sweep the fieldDemagnetise
Soft ironHard steel / alnico
Soft magnet. Its domains flip at small fields: the loop is narrow, so it magnetises and demagnetises easily with little energy lost per cycle. This is why soft iron is used in transformer cores and electromagnets.
Magnetisation M
0.00
Domains up
18 / 36
Remanence
M left at H = 0
Coercivity
reverse H that makes M = 0

Each domain here has its own switching field, so the loop emerges from simple rules: a domain flips up when H exceeds its threshold and down when H drops below minus its threshold. In between it keeps its direction, which is the memory (hysteresis).

Susceptibility
The magnetic susceptibility χ = M / H says how strongly a substance responds to a field H by acquiring magnetisation M. Diamagnetic χ is negative and tiny; paramagnetic χ is positive and small and falls as 1/T (Curie's law); ferromagnetic χ is large, and above the Curie temperature it follows χ = C / (T − TcT_cTc​).
JEE traps
  • Paramagnetic means unpaired electrons and weak attraction that vanishes with the field. Ferromagnetic means domains and permanent magnetisation.
  • Ferro-, antiferro- and ferrimagnetic solids all become paramagnetic above their Curie or Néel temperature.
  • Ferrimagnetic: opposite, unequal moments (net moment, Fe₃O₄). Antiferromagnetic: opposite, equal moments (net zero, MnO).
  • A species with all electrons paired is diamagnetic. Count unpaired electrons from the electronic configuration, then use √(n(n+2)).

10.1 Origin of magnetic moments

Magnetism arises mainly from electron orbital motion and electron spin. In many transition-metal and lanthanide compounds, partially filled shells carry permanent moments. In closed-shell species, applied fields induce small opposing currents that produce diamagnetism.

μ=−gμBJℏ\boldsymbol{\mu}= -g\mu_B\frac{\mathbf{J}}{\hbar}μ=−gμB​ℏJ​

For many first-row transition-metal ions in complexes where orbital angular momentum is substantially quenched, the spin-only approximation is useful.

μso=n(n+2) μB\mu_{so}=\sqrt{n(n+2)}\,\mu_Bμso​=n(n+2)​μB​

nnn is the number of unpaired electrons.

10.2 Magnetic field quantities and susceptibility

Magnetisation MMM is magnetic dipole moment per unit volume. In a linear material, it is proportional to applied magnetic field strength HHH.

All matter is diamagnetic at some level

Paramagnetism or cooperative ordering usually dominates when unpaired electrons are present. Diamagnetism remains as a smaller background contribution.

10.3 Diamagnetism and paramagnetism

Diamagnetic substances contain no required permanent net moment in zero field and develop an induced moment opposite to the applied field. Their susceptibility is nearly temperature independent. Paramagnets contain permanent moments that are randomly oriented without a field and partially align when a field is applied.

χ=CT\chi=\frac{C}{T}χ=TC​

10.4 Ferromagnetism and domains

In a ferromagnet, exchange interactions favour parallel alignment of neighbouring moments below the Curie temperature TCT_CTC​. A macroscopic specimen divides into domains to reduce magnetostatic energy. In an unmagnetised sample, domain magnetisations can cancel even though each domain is internally ordered.

An applied field moves domain walls and rotates domain moments. After the field is removed, some magnetisation can remain, producing hysteresis.

Hysteresis termMeaningMaterial implication
SaturationAll accessible domains alignedMaximum magnetisation
RemanenceMagnetisation at zero field after saturationHigh for permanent magnets
Coercive fieldReverse field required to reduce MMM to zeroLow for transformer cores; high for permanent magnets
Loop areaEnergy dissipated per magnetic cycleSmall for soft magnetic materials

Above TCT_CTC​, thermal disorder destroys long-range ferromagnetic order and the material becomes paramagnetic, often following a Curie–Weiss law.

χ=CT−θ\chi=\frac{C}{T-\theta}χ=T−θC​

For a ferromagnet, θ\thetaθ is generally positive and close to TCT_CTC​.

3
Worked example

Soft versus hard magnet

Which material is preferred for a transformer core: one with a narrow or wide hysteresis loop?

  1. The core is magnetised and demagnetised every ac cycle.
  2. Energy loss per cycle equals the loop area.
  3. A narrow loop also implies low coercivity.
A soft magnetic material with a narrow hysteresis loop is preferred.

10.5 Antiferromagnetism and ferrimagnetism

In an antiferromagnet, neighbouring sublattice moments align antiparallel with equal magnitude, giving zero ideal net magnetisation below the Néel temperature TNT_NTN​. In a ferrimagnet, sublattice moments are antiparallel but unequal, so a net moment remains.

OrderSublattice relationNet momentExamples
FerromagneticParallelLargeFe, Co, Ni
AntiferromagneticAntiparallel and equalIdeally zeroMnO, NiO, Cr2_22​O3_33​
FerrimagneticAntiparallel and unequalNon-zeroFe3_33​O4_44​, ferrites MFe2_22​O4_44​

In magnetite, Fe3+^{3+}3+ moments on tetrahedral and octahedral sites largely cancel, while Fe2+^{2+}2+ moments on octahedral sites produce the net ferrimagnetic moment in the simplified ionic picture.

Paramagnetic does not mean non-interacting forever

A material can be paramagnetic above an ordering temperature and become ferro-, antiferro- or ferrimagnetic below it.

Worked example

Defect plus magnetism

Fe1−x_{1-x}1−x​O contains Fe2+^{2+}2+ and Fe3+^{3+}3+. Why does increasing xxx alter both conductivity and magnetism?

  1. More cation vacancies require more Fe3+^{3+}3+ for charge balance.

Worked example

Semiconductor and defect chemistry

Oxygen-deficient ZnO is commonly n-type. Connect the defect reaction to its conductivity.

  1. Oxygen loss creates oxygen vacancies and leaves electrons.
  2. The electrons enter donor-like/conduction states.
  3. Electrons become majority carriers.
Oxygen vacancies generate electrons, producing n-type conductivity.

Radius ratio and pressure

A salt changes from NaCl-type to CsCl-type under high pressure. Explain the coordination change.

  1. NaCl type has CN 6; CsCl type has CN 8.
  2. High pressure favours structures with higher coordination and often higher density.
  3. The rigid ambient-pressure radius-ratio chart cannot alone describe compressed ions.
Pressure stabilises the denser 8-coordinate CsCl-type arrangement.

Revision strategy

For any numerical problem, first identify the structural model and write one geometrical relation, one counting relation and one physical-property relation. Most difficult-looking questions reduce to a controlled combination of these three.

10.10 Critical fields and magnetic measurement

For an ideal Type I superconductor, a commonly used empirical temperature dependence of the thermodynamic critical field is

Hc(T)=Hc(0)[1−(TTc)2]H_c(T)=H_c(0)\left[1-\left(\frac{T}{T_c}\right)^2\right]Hc​(T)=Hc​(0)[1−(Tc​T​)2]

Type II superconductors instead possess lower and upper critical fields Hc1H_{c1}Hc1​ and Hc2H_{c2}Hc2​, with quantised vortices in the mixed state between them.

MethodWhat it measures

Faraday balanceMagnetic force on a small sample in a field gradient

Measurement sign

Diamagnetic samples are driven toward weaker field; paramagnetic samples toward stronger field in a field gradient.

PART 8

Going deeper: defect chemistry and structure types

Extra depth in the style of a university solid-state course: the notation chemists use for defects, how doping is balanced, when a perovskite is stable, how spinels split their cations, and why only some rotation symmetries exist.

Everything in this part is original working in the same spirit as a university course (for example A. R. West, “Solid State Chemistry and its Applications”). The ideas are standard; the wording, numbers and figures here are our own. Use them to answer unfamiliar questions: the reasoning, not the memorising, is what the JEE Advanced paper rewards.

1. Writing defects: Kröger–Vink notation

A defect is written as a symbol with a subscript (the site it sits on) and a superscript (its effective charge, measured against what the perfect lattice has there). A dot • means one unit of effective positive charge, a prime ′ means one unit of negative charge, and × means neutral. The letter VVV stands for a vacancy and the subscript iii for an interstitial position.

SymbolMeaningWhy that charge
V_Na′Vacancy on a Na⁺ siteAn empty Na⁺ site has 1 unit of positive charge missing, so it is −1 compared with the perfect crystal
V_Cl•Vacancy on a Cl⁻ siteRemoving a −1 ion leaves +1 compared with the perfect crystal
Ag_i•Ag⁺ squeezed into an interstitial siteThe interstitial position is empty in the perfect lattice, so an Ag⁺ there is +1
Na_Na^×, Cl_Cl^×Normal ions on their own sitesNo change, so neutral
Sr_Na•Sr²⁺ on a Na⁺ site+2 where +1 is expected, so +1
Y_Zr′Y³⁺ on a Zr⁴⁺ site+3 where +4 is expected, so −1
V_O••Oxygen vacancy in an oxideRemoving O²⁻ leaves +2
e′, h•A free electron and a holeElectron −1, hole +1
Three rules for writing a defect reaction
Mass balance (same atoms each side), charge balance (the effective charges add to zero) and site balance (the ratio of cation to anion sites must stay as in the perfect crystal; a vacancy counts as a site). A perfect lattice creating defects from nothing is written as null → …

2. Solid solutions and doping with a different charge

A solid solution is a crystal where a second substance dissolves in the host without changing its structure. If the two ions have the same charge and similar size (Hume-Rothery: radii within about 15 %), they mix freely, as in Al₂O₃–Cr₂O₃ (ruby). If the charges differ (aliovalent substitution), the crystal must compensate, either by making vacancies or interstitials (ionic compensation) or by changing the oxidation state of another ion or creating electrons/holes (electronic compensation).

Derivation 8.1

Composition of yttria-stabilised zirconia (ZrO₂ with Y₂O₃)

Given
Zirconia ZrO2 is doped so that a fraction x of the zirconium sites hold Y3+ ions. The fluorite structure keeps all cation sites occupied.
To find
The formula of the solid solution and the fraction of oxygen sites that are empty.
  1. 1
    Write the cation content: xxx of the cations are Y3+^{3+}3+ and 1−x1-x1−x are Zr4+^{4+}4+, so the total positive charge per formula unit is:
    (1−x)×4+x×3=4−x(1-x)\times 4 + x\times 3 = 4 - x(1−x)×4+x×3=4−x(1)
  2. 2
    The oxygen sites carry O2−\mathrm{O^{2-}}O2−. Let yyy be the number of oxide ions per formula unit; the crystal is neutral when:
    2y=4−x;⇒;y=2−x22y = 4 - x ;\Rightarrow; y = 2 - \frac{x}{2}2y=4−x;⇒;y=2−2x​(2)
  3. 3
    Out of the two oxygen sites per cation, x/2x/2x/2 are therefore vacant. As a fraction of all oxygen sites:
    vacant fraction=x/22=x4\text{vacant fraction} = \frac{x/2}{2} = \frac{x}{4}vacant fraction=2x/2​=4x​(3)
Hence
Zr1−xYxO2−x/2;fraction of vacant O sites=x4\mathrm{Zr}_{1-x}\mathrm{Y}_{x}\mathrm{O}_{2-x/2};\qquad \text{fraction of vacant O sites} = \dfrac{x}{4}Zr1−x​Yx​O2−x/2​;fraction of vacant O sites=4x​∎

For x = 0.2 the formula is Zr0.8Y0.2O1.9 and 5 % of the oxygen sites are empty. Those vacancies let O²⁻ ions hop, so the solid is an oxide-ion conductor used in fuel cells and oxygen sensors.

JEE traps
  • A vacancy is not 'nothing': it carries an effective charge, so a V_Na′ attracts a V_Cl• and they can form pairs.
  • Doping with a LOWER charge cation (Ca²⁺ in ZrO₂) gives anion vacancies; doping with a HIGHER charge cation (Sr²⁺ in NaCl) gives cation vacancies.
  • Solid solutions change the cell size smoothly with composition (Vegard's law), unlike mixtures of two phases, which give two sets of diffraction lines.

3. Perovskites and the tolerance factor

The perovskite family ABO₃ (CaTiO₃, SrTiO₃, BaTiO₃) has a large cation A in the centre of a cube, a small cation B at its corners, and oxygen at the edge centres, so each B is inside an octahedron of six O. The structure is only stable if the ions fit together, and the *tolerance factor* says whether they do.

Derivation 8.2

The Goldschmidt tolerance factor

Given
An ideal cubic perovskite ABO3 of edge a with A at the cube centre, B at the corners and O at the edge centres. All ions touch their neighbours.
To find
The ratio t that measures how well the ions fit together.
  1. 1
    B and O touch along a cell edge. B is at a corner, O at an edge centre, so the edge holds one B–O contact on each side:
    a=2 (rB+rO)a = 2\,(r_B + r_O)a=2(rB​+rO​)(1)
  2. 2
    A sits at the cube centre. It touches the nearest O, at an edge centre, which is half a face diagonal away:
    a22=rA+rO;⇒;a2=2 (rA+rO)\frac{a\sqrt2}{2}= r_A + r_O ;\Rightarrow; a\sqrt2 = 2\,(r_A+r_O)2a2​​=rA​+rO​;⇒;a2​=2(rA​+rO​)(2)
  3. 3
    Divide the second relation by the first. If the ions fit perfectly the ratio is exactly one; the departure from one is the tolerance factor:
    t=rA+rO2 (rB+rO)t=\frac{r_A+r_O}{\sqrt2\,(r_B+r_O)}t=2​(rB​+rO​)rA​+rO​​(3)
  4. 4
    Real structures are stable cubic for 0.9≤t≤1.00.9\le t\le1.00.9≤t≤1.0. Smaller ttt means A is too small and the octahedra tilt; larger ttt means A is too big and layers stack hexagonally.
Hence
t=rA+rO2 (rB+rO)t = \dfrac{r_A+r_O}{\sqrt{2}\,(r_B+r_O)}t=2​(rB​+rO​)rA​+rO​​∎

Worked check, SrTiO₃ (r_Sr = 1.44 Å, r_Ti = 0.605 Å, r_O = 1.40 Å): t = 2.84 / (1.414 × 2.005) = 1.00, ideal cubic.

Walk through step by step
TOLERANCE-FACTOR LAB (r(O²⁻) = 1.40 Å)
t=rA+rO2 (rB+rO)=1.002t=\dfrac{r_A+r_O}{\sqrt2\,(r_B+r_O)}=1.002t=2​(rB​+rO​)rA​+rO​​=1.002

t > 1: A is too big, so the B ion rattles and the cell tends to hexagonal stacking (BaNiO₃ type)

Try SrTiO₃ (1.44, 0.605), BaTiO₃ (1.61, 0.605) and CaTiO₃ (1.34, 0.605).

Why BaTiO₃ is ferroelectric
For BaTiO₃ ttt is slightly above 1: the Ti⁴⁺ ion is a little too small for its octahedral hole, so it sits off-centre. Two or more off-centre positions of equal energy give a permanent electric dipole that can be reversed by a field: this is ferroelectricity, and it is why BaTiO₃ is used in capacitors.

4. Spinels: two ways to fill the holes

The spinel AB₂O₄ (MgAl₂O₄, Fe₃O₄, ZnFe₂O₄) is built from a cubic close-packed array of O²⁻. For each O²⁻ there is one octahedral void and two tetrahedral voids, so a formula unit with four O has 4 octahedral and 8 tetrahedral voids. Only one tetrahedral and two octahedral voids per formula unit are occupied: one-eighth of the tetrahedral and one-half of the octahedral voids.

Derivation 8.3

Counting the cations in a spinel cell

Given
Spinel AB2O4 with O2− in ccp. One unit cell holds 8 formula units, i.e. 32 oxide ions.
To find
Where the 8 A and 16 B cations sit in a unit cell of 8 formula units.
  1. 1
    In a ccp array of NNN ions there are NNN octahedral and 2N2N2N tetrahedral voids. With N=32N=32N=32:
    octahedral=32,tetrahedral=64\text{octahedral}=32,\qquad \text{tetrahedral}=64octahedral=32,tetrahedral=64(1)
  2. 2
    The cell holds 8 formula units, hence 888 A and 161616 B cations, 242424 in total, filling 242424 of the 969696 voids.
  3. 3
    Normal spinel: all 8 A (M²⁺) in tetrahedral voids and all 16 B (M³⁺) in octahedral voids:
    864=18 of tetrahedral,1632=12 of octahedral\frac{8}{64}=\frac18\ \text{of tetrahedral},\qquad \frac{16}{32}=\frac12\ \text{of octahedral}648​=81​ of tetrahedral,3216​=21​ of octahedral(2)
  4. 4
    Inverse spinel: the 8 A ions and 8 of the B ions go in the octahedral voids; the other 8 B ions go in tetrahedral voids. Written B[AB]O4\mathrm{B}[\mathrm{AB}]\mathrm{O_4}B[AB]O4​ (tetrahedral ion first, octahedral ions in brackets).
Hence
normal: A[B2]O4;inverse: B[AB]O4\text{normal: } \mathrm{A}[\mathrm{B}_2]\mathrm{O}_4 ;\qquad \text{inverse: } \mathrm{B}[\mathrm{AB}]\mathrm{O}_4normal: A[B2​]O4​;inverse: B[AB]O4​∎

Which form wins depends on crystal-field stabilisation energy: ions with a large preference for octahedral sites (Ni²⁺ d⁸, Cr³⁺ d³) push themselves into octahedral voids, forcing Fe³⁺ (d⁵, no preference) into the tetrahedral holes.

5. Fullerenes: carbon cages and their voids

Buckminsterfullerene C₆₀ is a hollow ball of 60 carbon atoms, each bonded to three others (sp² with some strain). The molecules pack in a face-centred cubic array, and like any close-packed solid they leave octahedral and tetrahedral voids that metal atoms can fill.

Derivation 8.4

Why every fullerene has exactly 12 pentagons

Given
A closed cage of V carbon atoms (vertices), E bonds (edges) and F faces, all faces being pentagons or hexagons, and each atom bonded to exactly three others.
To find
The number of pentagons, and the numbers of hexagons, bonds and faces in C60.
  1. 1
    Euler's rule for any closed polyhedron without holes:
    V−E+F=2V - E + F = 2V−E+F=2(1)
  2. 2
    Each atom has three bonds and every bond has two ends, so 3V=2E3V=2E3V=2E, i.e. V=23EV=\tfrac23EV=32​E. Let ppp be the pentagons and hhh the hexagons, so F=p+hF=p+hF=p+h. Count bond-sides: every bond borders two faces:
    5p+6h=2E5p + 6h = 2E5p+6h=2E(2)
  3. 3
    Substitute V=23EV=\tfrac23EV=32​E into Euler's rule to get F=2+13EF=2+\tfrac13EF=2+31​E, and multiply by 6:
    6p+6h=12+2E6p + 6h = 12 + 2E6p+6h=12+2E(3)
  4. 4
    Subtract 5p+6h=2E5p+6h=2E5p+6h=2E from this:
    p=12p = 12p=12(4)
  5. 5
    For C60: V=60V=60V=60, so E=32×60=90E=\tfrac32\times60=90E=23​×60=90 and F=2+30=32F=2+30=32F=2+30=32. Hence h=32−12=20h=32-12=20h=32−12=20.
Hence
p=12 pentagons always;C60:12 pentagons+20 hexagons, E=90, F=32p = 12 \text{ pentagons always};\quad \mathrm{C_{60}}: 12\text{ pentagons} + 20\text{ hexagons},\ E=90,\ F=32p=12 pentagons always;C60​:12 pentagons+20 hexagons, E=90, F=32∎

The 12 pentagons are what bend the flat graphite sheet into a ball. This is a good way to answer any 'how many pentagons/hexagons' question.

6. Why crystals have only 2-, 3-, 4- and 6-fold axes

Derivation 8.5

The crystallographic restriction

Given
A lattice in a plane with two neighbouring points A and B separated by the shortest lattice distance t. Suppose the lattice has an n-fold rotation axis through every point (angle θ = 360°/n).
To find
Which values of n are possible.
  1. 1
    Rotate B about A by +θ+\theta+θ to get B′B'B′. Rotate A about B by −θ-\theta−θ to get A′A'A′. Because the lattice has the axis everywhere, A′A'A′ and B′B'B′ are also lattice points.
  2. 2
    A′B′A'B'A′B′ is parallel to ABABAB. Resolve along ABABAB: its length is ttt minus the two projections, each tcos⁡θt\cos\thetatcosθ:
    A′B′=t−2tcos⁡θ=t (1−2cos⁡θ)A'B' = t - 2t\cos\theta = t\,(1-2\cos\theta)A′B′=t−2tcosθ=t(1−2cosθ)(1)
  3. 3
    A′B′A'B'A′B′ is a lattice vector parallel to ABABAB, so it must be a whole-number multiple of the shortest distance ttt (or zero). Call the integer mmm:
    1−2cos⁡θ=m;⇒;cos⁡θ=1−m21 - 2\cos\theta = m ;\Rightarrow; \cos\theta=\frac{1-m}{2}1−2cosθ=m;⇒;cosθ=21−m​(2)
  4. 4
    Since −1≤cos⁡θ≤1-1\le\cos\theta\le1−1≤cosθ≤1 the integer mmm runs from −1-1−1 to 333:
    cos⁡θ=1, 12, 0, −12, −1 ⇒ θ=360∘, 60∘, 90∘, 120∘, 180∘\cos\theta=1,\ \tfrac12,\ 0,\ -\tfrac12,\ -1\ \Rightarrow\ \theta=360^\circ,\,60^\circ,\,90^\circ,\,120^\circ,\,180^\circcosθ=1, 21​, 0, −21​, −1 ⇒ θ=360∘,60∘,90∘,120∘,180∘(3)
Hence
n=1, 2, 3, 4, 6 onlyn = 1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4,\ 6 \text{ only}n=1, 2, 3, 4, 6 only∎

Five-fold axes cannot tile a plane (pentagons leave gaps). They do appear in quasicrystals, which have order but no repeating unit cell, and in the C60 molecule, which is not a lattice.

Defects, electrical and magnetic behaviour

TopicRemember
SchottkyMissing cation + anion pair; density decreases; NaCl, KCl, CsCl, AgBr
FrenkelIon moves to an interstitial site; density unchanged; ZnS, AgCl, AgBr

Method for any numerical
1) Identify the lattice and write Z. 2) Write the contact condition to link a and r. 3) Convert a to cm (1 pm = 10⁻¹⁰ cm). 4) Apply ρ = ZM / (a³N_A) or η = Z·(4/3)πr³ / a³. 5) Check the result against the known values before you move on.
JEE traps
  • Z is not the number of atoms in the picture. FCC shows 14, owns 4.
  • CsCl is simple cubic, not BCC. ZnS is 4 : 4, CaF₂ is 8 : 4, Li₂O is 4 : 8.
  • Frenkel and Schottky are both stoichiometric. Schottky lowers the density; Frenkel does not.
  • A metal's σ falls on heating; a semiconductor's rises.
  • Ferro-, antiferro- and ferrimagnetic substances all turn paramagnetic above their transition temperature.
  • Counting voids: N close-packed atoms give N octahedral and 2N tetrahedral voids, in both HCP and CCP.
